n0.text: {Sensors picked up a weird growth at {place}. It's spreading fast in an inward spiral, covering nine hectares, and {instrument} says it's already doubled in size.|There's a massive, aggressive organism growing at {place}. It's closing inward like a tightening knot, and {instrument} shows it's expanding at an alarming rate.}

choices.text: {Walk to the centre|Head into the middle|Push toward the core|Advance to the center} of the spiral.
{Take a sample|Collect a specimen|Scrape off a sample|Bag a piece} from the edge.
{Burn a firebreak|Torch the perimeter|Ignite a controlled burn|Drop a thermal line} and watch what it does.

n0.emText: {Something's growing at {place} in a tight spiral that closes inward. It's the only living thing on the entire rock, and it's expanding way too fast for comfort.|You recognize this pattern-it's an aggressive growth enclosing something at the center. Whatever's in the middle, it's definitely trapped.}
n0.bubba: Bubba will not step on it. "It's growed itself inward, sugar. Roba ca se chiude 'ncoppa a quaccosa. Somethin's in there."

a.text: The growth gets {denser and quieter|thicker and quieter} towards the middle. {At the core, the growth has enveloped a solid object|In the dead center, the biomass has sealed around an alien relic|At the middle of the spiral sits an encased metal artifact} that it did not grow, and has been careful about it.

choices.text: Cut it out.
Leave it and log the position.

a.emText:
The growth goes quiet towards the middle, the way a street goes quiet outside a hospital.
At the centre it has grown around a thing it did not grow, patiently, over years, the way a hedge grows round a bicycle. Whatever is in there has been kept the way you keep a wallet in an inside pocket on a bad street.

b.text:
{The sample fights the knife.|The sample argues with the knife.} It's not tough; it is unwilling.
In the tube it goes on moving, and by the time the team is back at the lander it has arranged itself into the same spiral, {one centimetre|a centimetre|half an inch} across.

choices.text: Keep it aboard.
Put it back where it came from.

c.text:
The firebreak burns {a clean line|a clean lane} across the spiral's arm.
The growth does not try to cross it. It goes round, in both directions, and meets itself behind the away team in under {few} minutes.

choices.text: Stand and fight it back to the lander.
Drop everything and run.

a1.text: It comes free in {a wet handful|a wet double handful} of stems and what is inside has been kept alive, {on purpose|deliberately}, by something with no reason to keep anything alive.

a2.text: The team backs out along its own trail. Behind them the spiral closes over the gap at walking pace, and the centre is {exactly|precisely} where it was, and {exactly|precisely} as hidden.

b1.text: Sealed, monitored, and worth {a great deal|a good deal|rather a lot} to the right laboratory. The ship's biology bay is a livelier place than it was, and {nobody|no one} sleeps quite as well.

b2.text:
It is taken back and set down at the edge, and the whole spiral shifts a metre towards the lander {and then|then|and after that} stops, which everyone agrees to record as wind.
Something's left on {ground} where the sample lay.

c1.text: {It's not a plant|Whatever it is, it is not a plant} and it does not burn a second time.

c2.text:
{Everyone gets aboard.|Everybody gets aboard.} The sample kits, the cutter and one boot do not.
{leader} is last up the ladder and does not look back, and says afterwards that it was not chasing them, it was seeing them off.

n0.text:
The transmission is a voice, in a language the ship's tables get to eighty per cent of, and it is asking for help by name. Not the ship's name. {leader}'s.
The source is a shelter at {place}, dug in against {hazard} and holding pressure.

choices.text: Knock.
Cut the power to the shelter first.
Ask it how it knows the name.

n0.emText:
The voice is asking for help by name, and the name is yours, and it is using the one that only eight per cent of you can hear properly.
The tables get it to eighty per cent. The other twenty per cent is a sound like somebody saying a word into a coat. It has been saying it for a long time out of a shelter the size of a bus stop on a world with no bus routes.
n0.bubba: "It's sayin' your name," says Bubba, very quietly, on the ladder. "Nun rispunnere subito. Let it say it twice."

a.text:
{The door cycles before anyone touches it.|The door cycles before a hand goes near it.} Inside is one room, one chair, one light, and a person in a suit {two generations|a generation|three generations} out of date sitting with their back to the door.
They do not turn around. They say they have been practising this for {a long time|a good while|longer than anybody says}.

choices.text: Sit down and listen.
Turn the chair around.

b.text:
{The team traces the feed and pulls it.|The team follows the feed back and pulls it.} The shelter goes dark; the voice does not stop.
It has not been using the shelter's power for a {very|remarkably} long time. {It is being polite.|It has been being polite.}

choices.text: Go in anyway.
Strip the shelter for parts and leave.

c.text:
The question gets {a long pause|a very long pause}, at least that part was honest.
Then: it does not know the name. It knows the shape of whoever is listening, and it fits a name to it. It has been fitting names to listeners {since before this world had an atmosphere|since before there was air on this world}.

choices.text: Ask what it wants.
Stop transmitting. Walk away.

a1.text:
It takes {an hour|the better part of an hour|two hours}. They were on a survey that never filed, they have been alone since before the party was born, and they are not asking to be rescued. {They are asking to be remembered.|What they are asking for is to be remembered.}
They give {leader} everything they have left, which is not much, and it is more than the ship deserves.

a2.text: {The suit is empty|There is nobody in the suit} and has been empty for a {very|remarkably} long time, and the voice keeps talking out of the chair, out of the walls, out of the away team's own helmets.

b1.text: Inside is {lots} years of somebody's handwriting on {every flat surface|every flat surface in the place}, and at the end of it, in the last clear space by the door, an apology addressed to whoever came.

b2.text: Good hardware, well maintained, and the team is up and away in {ninety minutes|an hour and a half|two hours}. The voice is still on the band when the ship makes its burn out of orbit.

c1.text: It wants what it has always wanted, and it explains this at length, and none of it survives the trip back up as anything the crew can repeat. What survives is in {leader}'s hands, and {nobody|no one} remembers being handed it.

c2.text: {The band goes quiet.|The band goes flat and quiet.} The team walks back across {ground} in a silence that everybody is grateful for, and the shelter does not call after them, which is somehow the unkindest part.

choices.text: Cut into the pressure hull.
Follow the cable running out of the wreck.
Strip the wreck and leave.

n0.emText:
A distress carrier that has outlived two power plants, running out of a hull lying on {ground} like a piece of junk dumped on the rocks.
It is very tidy inside. That is the thing about wrecks that have been thought about: they are always tidier than the people who left them.
n0.bubba: Bubba pats the hull like a man patting a horse. "She's been dead a long time an' she's still hollerin'. Overo? That's somebody's mamma callin' 'em in for tea."

a.text: {You torch through the main hatch.|Cutting through the emergency airlock reveals the cargo deck.|Prying the blast doors open gives access to the hold.} {The interior smells of stale nitrogen and rusted plating.|Dead electronics and frozen condensation coat every surface.|Emergency lighting flickers in the gloom.}

choices.text: Open the locker.
Take the log recorder and go.

b.text: {Climbing into the upper superstructure brings you to the transmitter mast.|The access ladder leads directly to the beacon housing.|You scramble up the outer hull toward the antenna array.} {The beacon is buzzing loudly, radiating a greasy electromagnetic field.|Sparks spit from the damaged dish.|The transmitter is running hot despite the sub-zero cold.}

choices.text: Cut the mast down and take the core.
Point the mast at the ship and listen.

c.text:
The team works the wreck the way a wreck is meant to be worked: panels off, cells out, anything with a serial number into the bags. {It goes quickly.|It goes quickly enough.}
Halfway through, {instrument} shows {a second heat source|a second source of heat} under the hull.

choices.text: Dig it out.
Take what is in the bags and lift.

a1.text: {The seal gives.|The seal lets go.} Whatever the crew shut in there had been waiting with the patience of a thing that does not need to breathe, and it comes out at {leader} first.

a2.text:
The recorder comes out with its casing intact. Two hundred hours of watch reports, {and then|then|and after that} one voice, on the last day, saying that the ship is not where the ship thinks it is.
{Nobody|No one} opens the locker. The team is back aboard inside the hour.

b1.text: The core comes out of the mast {in one piece|whole|in a single piece}, heavier than it has any business being, and the distress carrier stops the moment it is clear of the housing. The silence afterwards is the loudest thing on the recording.

b2.text:
Turned around, the mast plays back the last {many} seconds of everything the away team has said, in their own voices, before they have finished saying it.
{leader} calls the walk short. The team comes up shaken and one of them will not talk about it.

c1.text: Under the hull is a reactor {the size of a barrel|no bigger than a barrel}, still lit, still governed, and salvage of that quality does not come along {twice|two separate times} in a career.

c2.text: The bags come up heavy with {cells, plate and cable|cells, plate, cable}. {Nobody|No one} looks at the second heat source again, and the ship is out of the system before anybody decides they should have.

n0.text:
{Zero solid ground anywhere.|No landing zones in sight.|Nothing but thick, churning atmospheric layers.} The signal comes from a fixed depth in {place}, {anchored dead still in an atmosphere that should crush steel|holding station against all logic|hovering in the middle of a toxic cloud bank}.
{It's either an automated relay station or someone very stubborn.|You're going to have to dive right into the soup to check it out.|Descending into that soup is definitely going to void the hull warranty.}

choices.text: Match its depth and hold.
Go below it and look up.
Grapple it and haul it up.

n0.emText:
No ground. The signal holds station at a fixed depth in {place} hovering dead still in the atmosphere.
You take the capsule down and the atmosphere closes over the ports at nine kilometres, and it does not feel like sinking. It feels like a lift going down into a building that has more basements than it has floors.
n0.bubba: "Nine kilometres," says Bubba, watching the ports go dark. "An' still goin'. Sto' palazzo tene troppe cantine, sugar."

a.text: {Descending through the atmospheric soup, the shape resolves:|Dropping lower through the clouds, you spot it:|Sensors clear up as you approach:} {an intact station|a massive floating platform|a floating industrial rig}, not a wreck, {anchored directly in the dense gas layers|holding station against the hurricane winds|silently humming with backup power}.

choices.text: Dock.
Photograph everything and climb out.

b.text: Below it the pressure is at the capsule's rating and the view up is {worth it|worth the rating}: the thing is not floating. It is standing on a column of something that goes down past the capsule, past the sounder's range, {past any floor this world has|past any bottom this world has}.

choices.text: Follow the column down.
{Take a sample|Collect a specimen|Scrape off a sample|Bag a piece} of the column and go.

c.text:
The grapple takes hold on the {second|third|first} pass. Whatever it is masses far less than it should and comes up easily for {six|five|seven} kilometres.
At six kilometres it stops coming, and the winch keeps running, and the cable keeps paying in.

choices.text: Keep winching.
Cut the cable.

a1.text: The dock takes the capsule like it was built for it, because it was. Inside there is air, and gravity, and a single corridor with a door at the end of it, and the door opens for {leader} and for {nobody|no one} else.

a2.text: Two hundred frames of a floating city that {nobody|no one} will believe, and a rise back through {hazard} that takes {many} hours and costs a heat shield.

b1.text: The capsule goes past its rating on the way to finding out what the column stands on. It comes back up with {two ports crazed|both ports crazed}, one crew member's ribs gone, and the answer, which {nobody|no one} has been able to write down.

b2.text: The sample arm comes back with three grams of the column in the pot, and the pot weighs {many} kilos, {and it is still cooling|and it has not finished cooling}.

c1.text: What comes up on the end of the cable is {not what the grapple took hold of|nothing like what the grapple took hold of}.

c2.text: The cutter takes the cable and the capsule goes up {like a cork|the way a cork goes up}. Snagged in the last metre of cable, still attached, is a plate of something that will not scratch.

n0.text: {The heat here will cook you alive in seconds.|The heat here will melt your suit seals in seconds.|The heat here will scorch your eyebrows off in seconds.|Thermal sensors are screaming at maximum.|The surface temperature is completely unhinged.} {The signal is transmitting out of the hottest point on the sweep.|Something is broadcasting directly from the center of the magma field.|A beacon is screaming from inside the hottest vent.}

choices.text: Go in with the suit at full cooling.
Send the drone in and stay out.
Wait for the cool phase.

n0.emText:
The heat here would finish an argument in under a second and something is transmitting out of the hottest point on the survey.
It's not hiding from the fire. It is plugged into it, the way a chip shop is plugged into a street: this is where the power is, so this is where you put your business.
n0.bubba: Bubba checks the suit seals four times, which for Bubba is a panic attack. "Somethin' down there's usin' the fire like a stove. Cucina, insomma."

a.text: {Approaching the magma vent, the radiation counters spike violently.|Heat shields glow cherry red as you push closer to the source.|The ground crunches like breaking glass under your boots.} {At the center of the caldera sits a glowing cylinder, totally unfazed by the lava.|The source is a solid metal beacon submerged in molten rock.|An alloy housing sits in the middle of the magma flow.}

choices.text: Reach out to it.
Get out while the suit still holds.

b.text:
The drone lasts {few} minutes, which is three and a half more than expected, and sends back a picture of {remnant} standing in the fire, unmarked.
Then something takes the drone. Gently. The signal ends without breaking up.

choices.text: Go and get the drone back.
Log it as lost.

c.text:
The cool phase comes {many} hours later and lasts {lots} minutes, and the team walks in over ground that is merely lethal.
The source is a cavity, and the cavity is lined, and the lining is not natural.

choices.text: Strip the lining.
Get inside the cavity.

a1.text: The glove does not burn. Something's put into it, {deliberately|on purpose}, by something with no hands, and {leader} walks out of the heat carrying an object that is cold.

a2.text: The suit holds all the way out and fails in the airlock, which is {the best possible place|the one good place} for a suit to fail. The scans taken on the way are worth the replacement.

b1.text: The drone is at the edge of the heat, {set down facing outwards|set down with its face turned outwards}, with its recorder full and its casing packed with something that should not exist at that temperature.

b2.text: The loss goes in the log with the rest of the year's losses. The {few} minutes of footage get {quietly|without fuss} copied by three separate people before the ship reaches the next system.

c1.text: It peels off in sheets, {light as foil|as light as foil}, and every sheet holds temperature like it has an opinion about it. There is enough here to line a ship.

c2.text: The cavity is occupied, and the cool phase is not a phase. {It is a habit|It is a habit of the place}, and the away team has just walked into the middle of it.

n0.text: {A graveyard of {vessel} hulls scattered across {ground}.|Dozens of dead {vessel} wrecks littering the area.|A junkyard of broken hulls rusting on {ground}.} {Nobody came back for them.|Every single one was stripped of parts years ago.|It's basically a monument to bad piloting.} {instrument} flags {one ship with a live signature|a faint power reading in the largest wreck|a working distress transponder in the rubble}.

choices.text: Board the oldest.
Board the newest.
Find out who does the sweeping.

n0.emText:
{many} ships moored in a row at {place}, none of them from any registry the ship carries, all of them parked rather than wrecked.
Somebody sweeps between them. It is a car park. It is a residents' car park on a world with no residents, and the bays are marked, and yours is not one of them.
n0.bubba: Bubba counts the moorings. "They's all parked nice. Nisciuno ha parcheggiato malamente. That's the part I don't like."

a.text:
The oldest is stone, or something that has become stone, and its hatch is a hole cut {by hand|by somebody's hand} from the outside.
The inside is one room, {and the room is a nest|and the room has been made into a nest}, and it has been used since long after the ship stopped flying.

choices.text: Search the nest.
Wait outside for whatever lives there.

b.text:
The newest has been here {many} years by its own clock and its hull is in better order than the party's own ship.
The crew log ends {on the day they arrived|the day they arrived|on their day of arrival}, mid-sentence, in the middle of a supply count.

choices.text: Take the ship's stores.
Try to bring the ship back up.

c.text:
The sweeping is done {at a set hour|to a set hour|on the hour, every time}, and the away team is in cover for it.
What comes out to sweep is small, and old, and does the whole anchorage in {ninety minutes|an hour and a half}, and stops at each ship to check the mooring line.

choices.text: Offer it a mooring line of your own.
Follow it home.

a1.text: Under the bedding there are {few} hundred small objects, {sorted by size|graded by size|laid out by size}, and every one of them came off a different ship. The best of them is the last one in the row.

a2.text: {It comes home at the end of its round|It comes back at the end of its round} and it is not pleased to find the door open.

b1.text: {many} years of stores, packed by people who {knew what they were doing|knew the work}, and the away team takes as much as the lander will lift.

b2.text:
The reactor lights on the {third|second|fourth} try and the ship comes up all the way, every board green, {and then|then|and after that} it will not release the moorings, and nothing on any panel explains why.
It is put back to sleep. It goes willingly.

c1.text: It takes the line, tests it, coils it {properly|correctly}, and moors the lander with it, {and then|then|and after that} it hands {leader} the thing it has been carrying since the first ship arrived.

c2.text: Home is a hole under the anchorage, and inside it is every mooring line that has ever failed, {spliced back together|spliced whole again}, and the tools that did the splicing.

n0.text: {The ground underfoot sounds hollow, like walking on a rusted tin roof.|Subsurface radar shows massive empty cavities directly below {place}.|The crust here is paper-thin and honeycombed with tunnels.} {Something is broadcasting from sixty meters down.|A clear transmission is pulsing from inside the subterranean void.|Audio sensors pick up metallic clicks echoing from below.}

choices.text: Go down the shaft.
Sound the whole body first.
Blow the shaft wider and send the drone.

n0.emText:
The body weighs a third of what it should and the survey pulse comes back off an inside face.
It is a shell with a room in it. Every so often the universe turns out to have been built by a landlord: a nice frontage, and behind the frontage a stairwell with somebody living in it.
n0.bubba: "A shell," says Bubba, kicking the collar of the shaft. "'Nu palazzo cu 'na sola scala. Somebody's home, sugar, an' the door's open."

a.text:
{few} hundred metres of shaft, {and then|then|and after that} it opens out. The inside of the body is a single space with a floor curving up on all sides, and it is not empty.
There is weather in here. There should not be weather in here.

choices.text: Cross to the middle.
Keep to the wall and map it.

b.text:
Sounding takes {a day|a whole day|two days} and turns up the shape of it: chambers, and passages between chambers, and one chamber that returns nothing at all, {as though the pulse goes in and stays|as though the pulse goes in and does not come out}.
{wrongness}.

choices.text: Open the silent chamber.
Mine the ones that answered.

c.text: The charge opens the collar and the drone goes down with the light on. It sends back {many} minutes of an interior {nobody|no one} will ever be allowed to visit, {and then|then|and after that} its telemetry ends mid-frame, without any of the usual warnings.

choices.text: Go down after it.
Sell the footage and never come back.

a1.text: At the middle is the thing the whole body was built around, hanging at the centre of gravity, {turning slowly|turning, slowly|turning at a walking pace}, and it lets {leader} take one piece of itself without any argument at all.

a2.text: The map takes {six|five|eight} hours and is worth every minute: a complete interior survey of an artificial world, with the machinery of it laid bare along the wall like an anatomy.

b1.text: {It's not a chamber.|That is not a chamber.} It is an occupant, and it has been folded into that space for longer than the body has been in this orbit, and it unfolds.

b2.text: {The answering chambers are stores|The chambers that answered are stores}, and the stores are full, and whoever packed them expected to come back for them.

c1.text: The drone is {lots} metres down, undamaged, and pointing back up the shaft. Something set it down {carefully|with care}, and put something next to it, and left.

c2.text: {many} minutes of the inside of a hollow world sells for {what a small moon sells for|the price of a small moon}. The buyer does not give a name and does not haggle, which is its own kind of answer.

n0.text: {The scanner is picking up an exact duplicate of {vessel}'s transponder signature.|Something down on {ground} is broadcasting our exact ship ID and callsign.|Sensor telemetry is mirroring our own ship data with zero delay.} {It's either a severe sensor glitch, a very weird relay, or someone trying to mock us.|Either the electronics are fried, or something down there is copying our homework.}

choices.text: Follow the other team's tracks.
Set up and wait for them to arrive.
Talk to them on the suit channel.

n0.emText:
Your own suit telemetry, five channels, correct headers, correct names, arriving from {place} {many} minutes before you land there.
Somebody has already done this. Someone's doing it now, slightly ahead, wearing your headers. You are the last person in this universe entitled to be squeamish about a copy of a woman turning up where the original has not arrived yet.
n0.bubba: Bubba looks at the telemetry and then at you and puts his hand on your shoulder. "Whatever's wearin' our names down there, it ain't us. Ricordatelo. Whatever it says."

a.text:
The tracks are the away team's own boots, in the away team's own sizes, laid down in {ground} before the lander touched.
They lead away from the landing site, do everything the team is about to do, and stop.

choices.text: Walk to where they stop.
Do something the tracks did not do.

b.text:
{They arrive on schedule|They arrive exactly on schedule}, from the direction the telemetry said, five of them, in the same suits, walking the way the away team walks.
They stop {lots} metres out and wait to be spoken to.

choices.text: Trade with them.
Do not let them any closer.

c.text:
The channel is open both ways and the voice on it is {leader}'s, half a second early, getting every word right before it is said.
It asks the away team not to come to {place}. It is {very|remarkably} calm about it.

choices.text: Ask what happens there.
Go there.

a1.text: Where they stop there is a cache, packed by people {with the same hands|whose hands were the same as theirs}, and a note in {leader}'s handwriting that says only: it is worth it, take it, do not stay.

a2.text:
{leader} sits down in {ground} and refuses to move for {few} minutes, out of spite.
It works. The tracks stop being ahead of them. Everything since landing has to be done again, {properly|correctly}, and the team is tired in a way sleep does not touch.

b1.text: They trade fairly, and hard, and they know {exactly|precisely} what the team can spare, which is the most frightening thing about the whole exchange.

b2.text: {They come closer.|They come closer than that.}

c1.text: It tells them. It takes {four|three|five} minutes and the team does not go, and on the walk back the voice thanks them, once, and stops half a second before it should.

c2.text: At {place} there is nothing but {remnant} and a {very|remarkably} clear view, and everybody comes back, and the count is right, and the ship's log will record that the count was right.

n0.text: {The transponder signal is moving fast across {ground}, heading on a direct intercept course.|Something is tracking us, carrying an obsolete distress beacon as bait.|A fast-moving radar contact is closing the distance across {place}.} {It's not broadcasting for help; it's using the signal to hunt.|Whatever's carrying that beacon definitely isn't a stranded crew member.}

choices.text: {Set an ambush|Take cover and wait|Hide behind the rocks|Prepare an ambush} and wait for it.
{Circle round|Flank it from behind|Sneak up on its blind side|Come around the back} and come at it from behind.
{Broadcast on the same frequency|Hail them on the open band|Answer the signal|Open a comms channel}.

n0.emText:
A ship-standard transponder on a frequency nobody has used in decades, moving over {ground} on a line that will cross yours.
It stops when you stop. It has done this before and it has done it enough times to have got polite about it, the way a man following you home keeps a consistent distance so that neither of you has to say anything.
n0.bubba: "It stopped when we stopped," says Bubba. "Aoh. Nun e' curiosa. It's got a method."

a.text:
{Two hours|Three hours|An hour and a half} in cover at {place}. The transponder comes on at last light and it is being carried, not worn, by something the size of a lander leg that moves {like it has all the time in the world|as though nothing is chasing it}.
It is dragging a net, and the net is full.

choices.text: {Take the shot|Open fire|Pull the trigger|Shoot first}.
{Let it pass|Hold fire and wait|Stay hidden until it moves on|Let it walk by} and follow the net.

b.text:
{Coming at it from behind works|Coming up behind it works}, in that the team gets to see it before it sees them.
It is sitting in a scrape it has made for itself, and it is surrounded by suit helmets, arranged in a circle, {all facing inwards|every one facing inwards}.

choices.text: Take a helmet.
Back off quietly.

c.text:
{leader} keys the old frequency and says the standard hail.
The answer is the standard reply, word perfect, in {leader}'s own voice, and it is coming from {about|something like|roughly} sixty metres away.

choices.text: {Answer it again|Send another reply|Hail them back|Repeat the response}.
{Go to it|Approach the source|Move in closer|Head toward the signal}.

a1.text: {The first shot is good|The first shot goes exactly where it should} and does nothing at all except make it put the net down.

a2.text: It drags the net to a cache under an overhang and {stows it with the others|puts it away with the others}. There are {lots} years of others. The team lifts one and is gone before it comes back.

b1.text: There is a name {stencilled|stencilled in paint} inside the helmet and a recorder still in the collar with {many} seconds on it. Getting out with both is the hardest walking anyone does that year.

b2.text: {Nobody|No one} speaks until the lander hatch is shut. The transponder is still moving out there, and the ship logs the position, and marks the whole hemisphere as {a place to not go back to|somewhere nobody returns to}.

c1.text:
{Three|Four|Two} exchanges and it runs out of recorded phrases and starts making its own, badly, and the badness is what everybody remembers.
It leaves. It leaves a thing behind, on {ground}, halfway between.

c2.text: It has been waiting {a long time|a good while|longer than anybody says} for {somebody|someone} to walk towards it.

n0.text: {place} holds {an abandoned town|a ruined settlement|a cluster of collapsed stone buildings}. {Streets, broken drains, a central square, and {remnant} sitting in the middle.|A crumbling ghost town where nobody has lived for centuries.|Toppled archways and cracked stone foundations under a dead sky.}

choices.text: Go into the largest building.
{Follow the drains|Head down the drain tunnels|Climb down into the drainage conduit|Follow the sewer pipe} down.
Read the square.

n0.emText:
Streets, drains, a square, and {remnant} where a monument would go. Nothing burned. Nothing fell. They stopped, all at once, like a market at closing.
You walk down a road that was built to be walked down and every doorway you pass is the right size for you, which is either a coincidence or the single most frightening piece of information available on this world.
n0.bubba: Bubba stands in the middle of the square and turns round slowly. "Doors are our size. Steps are our size. Chi ll'ha fatte, sti scale?"

a.text:
It is a hall, and it is full of seats facing a stage, and on the stage is a machine that has been running the same {six|four|nine} seconds of something for as long as it has had power.
{Every seat is occupied.|Every seat in the hall is occupied.} They are not bodies. They are the shapes bodies leave in a room that has not been disturbed.

choices.text: Let the machine finish.
{Take the machine|Dismantle the device|Haul the hardware back|Pry the machine loose}.

b.text:
The drains are {dry, walkable|dry and walkable}, and better built than the streets above them. {Two hundred|Three hundred|A hundred and fifty} metres in they stop being drains and start being a corridor.
{sound}, from further along.

choices.text: {Keep going|Push deeper|Continue forward|Press on}.
Blow the tunnel entrance.

c.text:
{The square is a record.|The square itself is the record.} Every flat surface carries names, and the names are in columns, and the columns are dated, and the dates stop.
{leader} works out the last column is not a list of the dead. It is a rota.

choices.text: Check the names on the wall.
{Copy the record and go|Download the archives and leave|Grab the data and retreat|Log the data and extract}.

a1.text: It takes {nine|seven|eleven} minutes. It is a message, and it is an apology, and at the end of it the seats are empty in a way they were not before, and everybody in the away team feels it happen.

a2.text: It comes off the stage in {few} pieces and every piece is worth more than the lander. The hall is {very|remarkably} quiet on the way out, and the seats are still occupied.

b1.text: The corridor ends at a door that was locked from this side, by hand, {in a hurry|and in a hurry}, and whatever they locked in has had a {very|remarkably} long time to get used to the idea.

b2.text: The charge brings the roof down {neatly|cleanly|square} across the corridor mouth. On the walk back up, the team lifts a plate of worked metal out of the drain wall: a street sign, or a prayer.

c1.text: Whatever needed watching is under the square, it is still there, and the last name on the rota {never got relieved|was never relieved}. The team relieves them, in the only way left, and takes the post's kit up.

c2.text: {many} thousand names in the ship's archive, none of which can be pronounced. {Somebody|Someone} in the crew starts reading them out loud on the trip home, and does not stop.

n0.text: {At {place} stands an alien monument that clearly doesn't belong here, completely untouched by the local weather.|There's an intact structure at {place}, looking pristine despite being in the middle of a barren wasteland.|A strange, seamless monolith rises out of {ground}, completely clean of dust or corrosion.}

choices.text: {Walk in|Step through the entrance|Cross the threshold|Head inside}.
Toss some junk on the step.
Scan it from a safe distance.

n0.emText:
Something at {place} that nothing here could have made and nothing here has touched, and the ground around it swept clean by something that comes back to sweep it.
It is kept. Not worshipped: kept, the way a difficult relative's flat is kept, by somebody who comes round on a Tuesday, does what has to be done, and leaves before dark.
n0.bubba: Bubba puts his hat on, which he does when he is being respectful. "Somebody cleans this. So somebody's comin' back. Nun tuccammo niente 'e sbagliato."

a.text:
The inside is one room and the room is much larger than the outside allows. The far wall is {a long way off|further off than it can be} and there is a queue of {maker} standing at it, with their backs turned, in perfect order.
They have been standing there long enough to have worn {grooves|hollows} into the floor.

choices.text: {Join the queue|Stand in line|Wait your turn|Step into formation}.
{Take something from the wall and run|Grab a relic and sprint for the door|Rip hardware off the wall and bolt|Snatch a piece and retreat}.

b.text:
{leader} puts a ration tin on the step, because it is what there is.
The tin is gone before the team has walked ten paces, and in its place, arranged with care, is a set of tools that are the right size for hands {nobody|no one} aboard has.

choices.text: {Take the tools|Grab the salvage gear|Pocket the equipment|Take the hardware}.
{Leave them and put down something better|Trade for a better offering|Leave a higher-value item|Swap with a better piece of scrap}.

c.text:
{Three hours of scanning|After three hours running the sensors|Three hours of mapping data|Logging sensor sweeps for three hours} from {lots} metres out. The structure has no seams, no foundations, and a mass that changes depending on which way it is measured from.
On the way back, {leader} finds a track in {ground} that goes round the whole site. It is fresh.

choices.text: {Follow the track|Track the trail|Shadow the footprints|Follow the path}.
{File the survey and lift|Log the coordinates and lift off|Pack up the sensors and launch|Upload the report and extract}.

a1.text: {leader} stands in line for what the suit clock calls {few} minutes and the crew above calls six hours. At the front there is a slot, and whatever is on the other side of it takes one memory and leaves something in its place.

a2.text: {The queue turns around all|The whole queue turns around all} {at once|all at the same time|together}, and none of them are facing the way faces should face.

b1.text: They come apart and go together in ways the ship's workshop will be arguing about for months. Two of them are missing a use {nobody|no one} has found yet.

b2.text:
The second offering is {a photograph|a photograph out of somebody's locker}, which is the most expensive thing anyone is carrying.
What comes back for it is not an object. It is a length of quiet in the middle of the away team, and everybody who walks through it comes out of it well.

c1.text: The track goes round the site nine times {and then|then|and after that} straight out to a cache buried {a metre|two metres|a half-metre} down, packed and labelled by whoever does the sweeping, as though for collection.

c2.text: The survey is the most valuable document the ship has filed all year, and it will be argued over by people who were not there. {Nothing follows the lander up.|Nothing comes up after the lander.}

n0.text: {It's not a distress call. It's {tone}, broadcasting from {place} on an endless loop.|An automated transmission ({tone}) is pulsing from {place} every few seconds.|An automated transmission ({tone}) is pulsing from {place} every many seconds.|A rhythmic signal is broadcasting out of {place}, clear and unbothered by atmospheric static.}

choices.text: {Answer it in the same pattern|Echo the signal rhythm|Transmit the matching code|Mirror the transmission frequency}.
{Find the transmitter and open it|Locate the beacon and pry it open|Track down the transmitter hatch|Dig up the broadcasting unit}.
Jam it.

n0.emText:
Not a distress call: a count, going out of {place} for longer than the catalogue admits.
Counts are the oldest magic there is. Somebody said a number here and then kept saying the next one, and the universe took it seriously, and it has been going ever since like a tap somebody left running in an empty flat.
n0.bubba: "It's countin'," says Bubba. "An' it ain't stopped for us. Chill' sta' cuntanno pe' quaccheduno ato."

a.text:
{leader} keys the pattern back, one beat late, {deliberately|on purpose} wrong in the last place.
The count stops. Nine seconds later it starts again, corrected, and now it is answering the mistake rather than repeating itself.

choices.text: Keep the conversation going.
Shut the radio off and back away.

b.text:
The transmitter is buried in {ground} with only its collar showing, and the collar is a hatch. It opens by hand. It was built to open by hand.
Inside: a mechanism with no moving parts, and {remnant} laid neatly on top of it, like an offering.

choices.text: {Take the mechanism|Pry out the core assembly|Salvage the internal clockwork|Strip the mechanism for parts}.
{Take the offering and close the hatch|Grab the cache and seal the lid|Take the prize and lock the hatch|Pocket the goods and shut the door}.

c.text:
The jammer goes up on a tripod and the band flattens out. For {many} minutes there is nothing across the whole spectrum but the sound of the away team breathing.
Then {hazard} makes itself felt, and the count comes back at three times the power.

choices.text: {Hold the position and burn it out|Keep the jammer running at maximum|Overload the frequency until it pops|Burn out the transmitter}.
{Pull back to the lander|Retreat to the ship|Pack up and get to safety|Evacuate the area}.

a1.text: It takes {few} hours to build a shared count and another two to trade nouns. What is on the other end is not close, is not alive in any sense the team can use, and gives {leader} a set of coordinates as a gift for the trouble.

a2.text: {The radio goes dark.|The comms cut out completely.|Static dies on the channel.|The signal flatlines.|The radio goes dead.|The channel goes completely silent.|Dead air on the frequency.|The receiver drops to zero.} The count keeps on over {ground} behind them all the way back to the lander, and the team walks the last hundred metres faster than they walked the first.

b1.text: {It lifts out easily.|The assembly slides out smoothly.|It pops free without any resistance.|The module unlatches cleanly.|It lifts out without any trouble.} The count stops, and every instrument the away team is carrying reports the same time to the same tenth of a second for the first time since they left Earth.

b2.text: The hatch shuts {sweetly|cleanly|the way it should}, the way a well-made thing does. The count carries on, and the team goes up with something in a bag that {nobody|no one} has a word for yet.

c1.text: The jammer wins, {eventually|in the end|sooner or later}, and the source dies with a noise like {a held breath let go|a breath finally let out}. The team digs the emitter out of the slag afterwards: it is beautiful, and it is worth a fortune.

c2.text: Whatever the count belongs to gets to the lander {before the team does|ahead of the team}, and it is standing between them and the hatch when they come over the last rise.

n0.text: {Thousands of small machine drones are crawling across {ground} like iron ants.|A massive swarm of tiny autonomous automatons is busy dismantling {place}.|Automated salvage drones are crawling over {place} in tight, synchronized patterns.}

choices.text: Figure out what they're up to.
{Catch one|Snag a drone with a net|Trap one of the units|Grab a specimen}.
{Put something in their way|Drop an obstacle on their path|Block their line with a crate|Set down a barrier}.

n0.emText:
Thousands of machines, none bigger than a hand, working over {ground} at {place} on a job that has been running for centuries.
They ignore you completely. That is the insult and the information: a work party that has been told what the job is does not stop for a woman with no papers, and you have spent eleven months being exactly that everywhere you go.
n0.bubba: Bubba squats down among them and lets four of them walk over his boot. "They got a job. Tenene 'a fatica. Sugar, don't get in the way of folks workin'."

a.text:
{Two hours of surveillance|After watching for two hours|Two solid hours of observation|Watching the line for a couple of hours} and the pattern comes clear. They are not building. They are taking something apart, {very|remarkably} slowly, {very|remarkably} {carefully|with care}, and putting the pieces in order along a line that runs to the horizon.
The thing being taken apart is the world.

choices.text: {Follow the line|Track the cable|Trace the conduit|Follow the route} to the far end.
Take a piece off the line.

b.text:
It comes up in a glove {without a fight|without any argument}, folds its legs, and goes still.
Every other machine within sight stops at the same instant, and stays stopped, {and turns to face the glove|and every one of them turns to face the glove}.

choices.text: Put it down.
Pocket it and walk.

c.text:
{leader} sets a sample case down across their line and steps back.
The swarm stops at it, considers it for nine seconds, {and then|then|and after that} goes round. On the way past, one of them measures the case and writes the measurement on it.

choices.text: {Give them something worth measuring|Toss a high-tech tool into their line|Offer an alloy sample|Drop a piece of advanced composite}.
{Take the case back and leave them to it|Pick up your gear and walk away|Retrieve the case and back off|Pack your tools and leave}.

a1.text: The far end is a stack, sorted by material, {taller than the lander|higher than the lander}, and at the top of it is the first thing they ever took off this world, labelled in a notation that predates the swarm.

a2.text: The line closes the gap in {many} seconds and does not react otherwise. The piece is a machined block of something the ship's assay cannot name, and there are {few} hundred kilometres of them.

b1.text: The moment it touches {ground} the whole field goes back to work {as though nothing happened|as though nothing at all had happened}. Where it was standing there is now a small object that was not there before, and it is a gift, or a receipt.

b2.text: {few} hundred metres from the lander the field decides how it feels about theft.

c1.text: The cutter goes down on the line. They swarm it, measure it, take it apart, and put it back together {improved|better than it was}, and leave it on {ground} pointing at the lander.

c2.text: The case comes back with a number on it in a base {nobody|no one} uses, {and the swarm carries on|and the swarm goes back to work}, and the away team is up and gone before anybody has to find out what the number means.

e_ocean.title: {The Bell Buoy That Is Not On The Chart|Something Is Ringing Out There|A Door Painted On A Can}

n0.text:
{A bell is clanging out in the middle of nowhere, {distance}, where the charts swear there's only deep water.
Through the mist you spot a rusted buoy bobbing awkwardly in the swell. Someone welded an iron ladder onto the side and literally spray-painted a fake door with a real handle onto the metal.|There's a buoy out here in two hundred meters of open water, ringing like crazy. Up close, it's a beat-up rusted drum with a welded ladder and a painted door that shouldn't be there.|There's a buoy out here in four hundred meters of open water, ringing like crazy. Up close, it's a beat-up rusted drum with a welded ladder and a painted door that shouldn't be there.}
n0.emText: {A bell is clanging out across the water with an annoying, repetitive rhythm. The buoy is bobbing in the chop with a ladder welded on and a fake door painted onto the steel. In this line of work, weird doors are usually trouble.|The buoy rings out over the swell. Up close it has a ladder and a painted door with a real handle. Definitely suspicious.}
n0.bubba: Bubba leans over the rail with his hat in his hand. "Sugar, that's a door on a can. Uh-uh. Back home we got a word for openin' that, an' the word is {funerale|stupidaggine}."

Circle it once and read everything written on it.
Cut the buoy loose and tow it in.
Log the position and go on.

a.text:
The ladder is warm. Suspicious.
The painted door has a painted handle, and when you take hold of the paint your hand closes on brass. Inside is a stairwell, dry, lit, going down further than the water is deep. {sound|Somewhere below, a radio playing under a floor} comes up the stairs to meet you.
a.bubba: "Well, madonna santa," says Bubba, testing the top step with his boot. "Stairs in the ocean. Jamme, then. You first, on accounta you float better."

asides.nervous: {member} {sweats inside their helmet and asks how much air we have left|keeps looking back toward the lander with wide eyes|jumps at every creak in the hull|wonders aloud if we can just leave right now}

choices.text: Go all the way down.
Take what is on the first landing and get out.

b.text:
Three languages, four hands, and one of them recent.
A name and a date, twice. A tide table for a port that does not exist. A phone number with the {Britannia|Varlenia|Collective} code. And under the waterline, where you have to hang off the ladder to read it: {rumour}.

asides.scholarly: {member} {is already logging sensor anomalies with an annoyed grunt|scans the alloy and mutters about obsolete manufacturing dates|checks the survey records and complains about missing documentation|notes that the readings make zero thermodynamic sense}

asides.any: {member} {keeps an eye on the sensors and says nothing|watches the approach with a neutral squint|checks their holster with quiet efficiency|stands by the entryway, ready for trouble}

choices.text: Ring the number from the boat's set.
Note it all down and sell the notes to somebody who wants them.

c.text:
It cuts easier than it should, and it tows like something that wants to come.
Half a mile in, the bell stops. Two miles in, {a cormorant|a gull|something with too many joints} lands on it and stays there, facing the way you came. The harbourmaster at {region} takes one look and pays you to take it away again.

d.text:
You write the position in the log with the time next to it and you go on.
Two days later, in a bar in {region}, a man who says he is a hydrographer buys the page off you. He does not want the page. He wants to know if the bell was ringing on the swell or against it.
Against it, you tell him. He pays you and leaves without his coat.

a1.text:
Eleven landings down, the stairwell opens into a room with a table, a chair, a lamp and a sea chart with your own course pencilled on it in a hand you do not know, ending where you are standing.
On the table, in {relicWord}, is the thing the bell was for.
a1.emText:
Eleven landings down there is a table, a chair, a lamp, and a chart with your own course already drawn on it, ending under your feet. The pencil is still warm. Ninety-two per cent of your life is filed somewhere you cannot get to and somebody down here has better records than you do.
On the table, in {relicWord}, is the thing the bell was ringing for. It's not a spellbook. You check twice.
a1.bubba: "Don't touch the chart," says Bubba, touching the chart. "Mannaggia. Okay. Touched it."

a2.text:
The first landing is a store: rope, tinned food, a crate of lamp oil, and four boxes of the kind of hardware nobody sells to a boat.
You take what two of you can carry and you are back in daylight before the tide turns, which is the only sensible thing anybody has done all week.

b1.text:
It rings four times. Then a woman's voice, flat as a chart datum, says a bearing, a depth and a time, and hangs up.
You are at that bearing at that time because you are the kind of crew that turns up. Something comes up out of the dark to meet the boat, and it is not interested in talking about it.

asides.any: {member} {keeps an eye on the sensors and says nothing|watches the approach with a neutral squint|checks their holster with quiet efficiency|stands by the entryway, ready for trouble}

b2.text:
The Foundation office in {region} takes the whole notebook, gives you a receipt in a language that is not one of the four on the buoy, and pays you for it in {coin}.
They ask you to stop writing things down. They ask it very politely.

e_fields.title: {The Standing Crop|The Square They Never Cut|{lots} Paces On A Side}

n0.text:
The field was cut a month ago. One square of it is still standing.
{lots} paces on a side, corners sharper than any plough has ever managed, and inside it {sound_field}. Outside it, in the stubble, nothing at all is moving, not even the {crows|gulls|pigeons} that ought to be here.
There is a gate, and a farmhouse {distance}, and a tractor parked exactly where somebody stopped it.
n0.emText:
One square of crop still standing in a cut field, sides too straight to be an accident, and you can feel it the way you feel a held note: something in there has been left deliberately unharvested, the way you were left deliberately unfinished.
Inside it {sound_field}. Outside, the stubble is not doing anything at all. The tractor is parked where somebody stopped it and got out and did not come back for it.
n0.bubba: Bubba squints at the corners. "That's surveyed, sugar. Somebody paid a fella with a stick an' a chain. Uh-huh. That ain't fairies, that's paperwork."

asides.artistic: {member} says the standing square looks like a word with all the other letters mown off.
asides.any: {member} {keeps an eye on the sensors and says nothing|watches the approach with a neutral squint|checks their holster with quiet efficiency|stands by the entryway, ready for trouble}

choices.text: Walk into the middle of it.
Go and find whoever farms this.
Cut a sheaf and take it away.
Burn it, and stand upwind.

a.text:
The stalks {lean away|part|bend aside} as you come on and close again behind you, politely, like a crowd letting somebody through to the front.
In the middle there is a patch of bare packed earth with a hollow in it, about the size of {a sleeping dog|a sleeping child|something that sleeps curled up}. It is warm. The crop around the hollow has come up a second time this year, out of season, and it has come up heavy.

asides.nurturing: {member} puts a hand flat on the warm earth and keeps it there.
asides.paranoid: {member} {mutters that someone's definitely watching us from the shadows|checks their six three times and grips their holster|hisses that the signal frequency is rigged|whispers: "They knew we were coming. Look around."}

choices.text: Lie down in the hollow.
Dig it out.
Fill it in and walk away.

b.text:
The farmhouse smells of {smell}. The man there does not want to talk about the square.
He wants to talk about his father, who left it standing for {lots} years, and about the two dry summers that followed the one time it got cut. He talks with his hands flat on the table, the way you talk when the table is the only steady thing in the room.
He will pay for it to be left alone. He will pay a good deal more if somebody will go in and look and come back and tell him it is nothing.
b.bubba: Bubba is already eating this man's bread. "Signo', don't you fret. We're professionals. Mostly her. Uh-huh."

asides.empathetic: {member} {looks at the wreckage and shakes their head: "Tough way to go."|checks for survivor logs with a quiet sigh|hopes whoever was here got out in time|mutters a quiet condolence for the crew}

asides.grumpy: {member} {complains loudly about the freezing temperature|curses under their breath at the terrible footing|mutters that this job isn't worth the hazard pay|kicks a piece of debris and grunts in frustration}
asides.any: {member} {keeps an eye on the sensors and says nothing|watches the approach with a neutral squint|checks their holster with quiet efficiency|stands by the entryway, ready for trouble}

choices.text: Take his money to leave it standing.
Take his money to go and look.
Take his tools and cut it flat.

c.text:
The sheaf comes away easily, like something handed over.
It stays green for {many} days in a pack where bread goes mouldy in three. The grain is heavier than the grain around it and it seeds true. The agricultural office in {region} takes the whole sheaf, asks no questions worth answering, and pays on the spot rather than by the usual cheque in April.

e.text:
It goes up like it was waiting to.
The fire keeps the square. It burns to the exact edge and stops, and what walks out of the middle of it is on fire too, and does not appear to consider that a problem worth discussing with you.

asides.aggressive: "There," says {member}, with enormous satisfaction, about four seconds too early.
asides.any: {member} {keeps an eye on the sensors and says nothing|watches the approach with a neutral squint|checks their holster with quiet efficiency|stands by the entryway, ready for trouble}

a1.text:
It is the length of a person and it fits the way a coat fits when somebody has had it made for you.
{leader} is out for {many} minutes by the watch and comes up with a taste of copper, a scar closed that has been open since the spring, and everybody standing over them looking rested for the first time in a month.
a1.emText:
It is the length of a person, and it fits you the way nothing has fitted you since the first of January.
You are out for {many} minutes. You do not get a memory back. You get the shape of one, the dent where it was, and something in the field turns over in its sleep and gives you back a scar closed and a night's rest you did not pay for.
a1.bubba: Bubba is holding your hat when you come up. "Nah, don't say nothin'. You was smilin'. Ain't seen that. Uh-uh."

a2.text:
{A foot down|Two feet down|Half a spade down}, the earth stops being earth.
What comes up out of the hollow has slept through several harvests and it wants {the rest of its year|the rest of the year it is owed|the winter it was promised}. It's not angry. It is worse than angry: it is awake early.

a3.text:
You fill the hollow with the loose earth around it and tread it down, and the crop closes over the top of it, and the field lets you leave.
The farmer will not take a penny back off you. In the yard he gives you {payment} instead and stands in the road watching until you are out of sight.

b1.text:
He pays in notes his father kept back from {three|two|four} good years, and shakes every hand twice.
The square is still standing. Everything around it will be, too, and in a bad year three villages will not know why they came through it.

b2.text:
You cut it in an afternoon, with his own machine, and he watches from the gate with his cap in his hands.
The grain fills more sacks than the field has any business filling. It sells for a great deal. The following spring is very dry, and the spring after that is worse, and nobody in that parish ever says your name out loud again, though they all know it.

e_meadows.title: {The Long Grass Nobody Cuts|Four Acres Left Standing|The Bench By The Stone}

n0.text:
The meadow has not been cut in years, and it should have been: it is good ground, and there is a farm on it, and the farm is working.
What stops the mower is halfway out: a stone, waist-high, with a bench next to it, and the bench is new. Somebody replaces that bench. Somebody has been replacing it for a while, judging by the four sets of post holes.
{smell}, and in the grass, {sound}.
n0.emText:
Good ground, uncut for years, and a stone in the middle of it with a bench next to it that somebody keeps replacing.
You can feel the shape of the arrangement without being told: this is a place where a thing was agreed, and the agreement is still running, and the grass is the payment. You know about agreements you cannot remember making.
n0.bubba: "Somebody's grandma sits here," says Bubba, sitting on it. "Ooh. Comodo. Nah, I'm stayin'."

asides.calm: {member} sits down on the bench and lets the meadow get on with whatever it is doing.

Read the stone.
Cut a swathe through the meadow with whatever is in the pack.
Go to the farm and ask.

a.text:
You wait an hour and a half and {stranger} comes up the track with a folding stool, sees the bench occupied, and sits down on the stool instead without complaint.
They have brought {food} for two. They offer you half without being asked and without looking at you.
"You'll want to be gone by dark," they say, comfortably. "It's not that it minds. It's that it forgets you're people."

asides.empathetic: {member} {looks at the wreckage and shakes their head: "Tough way to go."|checks for survivor logs with a quiet sigh|hopes whoever was here got out in time|mutters a quiet condolence for the crew}

choices.text: Stay past dark with them.
Ask what the arrangement is, plainly.

b.text:
No name. No date. A line of letters cut with a chisel by somebody who was not a mason, and under them, more recently, in paint: {rumour}.
The stone is warm on the north face and cold on the south, which is the wrong way round for a sunny afternoon, and has been the wrong way round for as long as anybody has been coming here with a bench.

choices.text: Dig at the base of the stone.
Copy the letters and take them to somebody who reads that sort of thing.

c.text:
You get four metres in.
The grass is not grass all the way down: at the root it is threaded through with something white and fine, and it goes taut when you cut it, all across the meadow at once, like a net being taken up.
The farm dogs start, a mile off. Then they stop, all together.

d.text:
The farmer is a woman in her sixties who does not put the kettle on, which tells you where you stand.
"It's four acres," she says. "Four acres is nothing. My mother did the same and her mother did the same and I've a good crop off everything else, haven't I."
She pays you not to write about it. She pays in cash and in {payment}, and she watches the meadow the whole time she is talking to you.

a1.text:
After dark the meadow does something with sound: everything you say arrives about a second late and from slightly the wrong direction.
{stranger} keeps talking anyway, calmly, into the dark, and at some point stops talking to you and starts talking to something else. Whatever answers uses your voice, which they seem to expect, and which they do not appear to think is worth mentioning.
In the morning there is dew on everything but the bench, and something in your pack that was not there.

a2.text:
"The grass stands, and it keeps the rest of the farm right. That's it. That's the whole of it."
They say it the way people say the rules of a game they have played all their life. Then they teach you the two things you do if you are ever caught in the middle of it at dark, and make you say them back, twice, and correct you once.

b1.text:
Nine inches down, the chalk is packed with small brown bones, all of them bird, all of them arranged.
A foot further, in {relicWord}, is the thing the arrangement was made over. It comes out clean and the hole fills itself in behind it with a sound like somebody sitting down.

b2.text:
A woman in {region} who restores church plate reads it in about four seconds and then will not read it again.
She pays you for the rubbing, which she burns, and for the promise that you will not go back, which she cannot enforce and which you make anyway.

e_forest.title: {The Blind|Somebody Is Sitting In The Trees|{landmark}}

n0.text:
The track in is better kept than the road that brought you to it. Somebody grades it. Nobody admits to it.
Half a mile in there is a hide up in a beech: a shooting blind, boarded, with a ladder and a felt roof and a stove pipe. It faces {landmark}. Zero game here worth a stove.
The ladder has been used this morning. In the trees, {sound}.
n0.emText:
The track is graded and the wood is quiet in the way a room is quiet when someone has just stopped talking about you.
There is a hide up a beech, boarded, with a stove pipe, facing {landmark}, and no game here worth sitting out for. Somebody watches this place professionally. You have been in the world eleven months and you already know what a professional watcher's chair smells like from underneath.
n0.bubba: Bubba looks up the ladder and back at you. "Deer blind. Sure. An' I'm the Pope. Nun c'e' sta niente 'a cacciare ccà, sugar."

choices.text: Climb up.
Go and stand in whatever the hide is watching.
Wait in the brush until somebody comes back for it.
Follow the graded track to whoever grades it.

a.text:
Warm stove. A flask, still hot. A camp stool, a pair of very good field glasses, and a logbook.
The logbook is not a game book. It is a list of dates and times and, in the third column, one word each: names, mostly. Some of them are names of people. Some of them are names of days.
Today's date is at the bottom. The third column has been filled in already, and the word is yours.
a.bubba: Bubba reads over your shoulder and goes very quiet, which from him is an alarm. "Sugar. Uh-uh. Chill' ccà nun so' cacciatori."

choices.text: Take the logbook and go.
Sit in the stool and wait for the owner.
Write a fourth column of your own.

b.text:
You walk out into the middle of what the glasses are pointed at, which is {landmark}, and you stand there, and nothing happens for four full minutes.
Then the birds stop. Not all at once: in a ring, closing, the way silence goes across a room when the wrong person comes in.

Speak first. Say what you are doing here.

c.text:
Two hours in the wet brush, and then somebody comes: not up the track, out of {landmark}, walking as if the wood were a corridor in their own house.
They climb the ladder, they light the stove, and they open the logbook. Then they lean out of the hide, look directly at where you are lying, and wave you in for tea.

choices.text: Go up and have the tea.
Leave, quickly, while they are being polite.

d.text:
The track ends at a forestry hut with a Britannia licence plate on a Varlenian van and a woman doing paperwork on the bonnet.
She is not surprised. She has a folder with your route in it, drawn in the same pencil the chart on the buoy was drawn in, if you have ever seen one of those.
"Two questions," she says. "Then either you work for us this afternoon or you never came up this track."

choices.text: Work for her this afternoon.
Never came up this track.

asides.authoritative: {member} {barks out orders to secure the perimeter|demands status reports on the double|reminds everyone to maintain radio discipline|takes charge of the entry team with a brisk nod}
asides.cynical: {member} {snorts: "Great. More overpriced scrap."|rolls their eyes: "Ten credits says there's nothing useful inside."|scoffs: "If there was anything valuable here, someone would have stolen it already."|shrugs: "Let's just grab the loot before something explodes."}

a1.text:
You are three miles off before you look at the earlier pages properly.
It is a register of everybody who has come up that track for nineteen years, and what became of them, and the last column for most of them reads the same short word. The Foundation office in {region} buys it off you in a corridor, standing up, and pays what it costs to make you stop asking about the word.

a2.text:
You sit in a dead man's stool for an hour and forty minutes and then the ladder creaks and somebody comes up who is not carrying a rifle.
What you talk about is the third column. What they leave you with, because you sat and waited instead of running, is {relicWord} out of the stove bench, and a rule about this wood you will use twice more this year.

a3.text:
You write down what each of them was wearing.
It takes twenty minutes and it is the most petty thing anybody in this party has done all month, and the wood does not like it. Something comes up the ladder that does not use the rungs.

b1.text: It comes out of the trees at a walk, on the wrong number of legs for the sound it was making, and it has been eating what the hide was for.

b2.text:
You say your name and your business, out loud, to a wood.
The ring stops closing. Something the size of a door leans out of the dark to look at you, decides, and goes away, and the birds come back on one after another like lights.
Where it stood there is a gap in the leaf litter with something in it that was pressed into the earth by weight and time.

c1.text:
Tea in a hide with a stranger who has been watching this wood for nineteen years and has never once been paid for it.
They tell you what the third column means, and what to do if you ever see your own name in it, and then they give you {payment} and put you back on the track facing the right way.

c2.text:
You go, and the wood lets you, and behind you the stove smoke comes up straight in a wind that is bending every tree it passes.
On the road you find the flask in your pack. Nobody put it there. It is still hot in {region}, four hours later, and it is still hot the next morning.

d1.text:
The afternoon's work is carrying four sealed boxes from {landmark} to the van without stopping, resting, or putting them down on ground.
You earn every note of it. One of the boxes is warm on one side and something in it moves when you take the corner.

d2.text:
You never came up that track. She writes that down too, in the folder, and thanks you sincerely.
What you take away is the sight of what was in the open folder: a map of this wood with nineteen hides on it, and a note in the corner about which of them are still manned.

e_forestice.title: {The Long Cold|Woodsmoke And No Chimney|Ninety Trees Marked In Blue}

n0.text:
Snow to the knee between black trunks, and ninety trees marked in blue paint at chest height, in a line that runs straight through a wood that has nothing straight in it.
There is woodsmoke. Zero chimney, no hut, no track, and no footprints but yours, and the smoke is coming up out of the snow itself about {distance} along the line.
n0.emText:
Ninety trees marked in blue, dead straight through a crooked wood, and woodsmoke coming out of the snow where nothing is burning.
Somebody drew a line here and the world took it seriously. You know how that works. You were a line somebody drew once, and the world took you seriously too, and look at you now.
n0.bubba: Bubba puts his hand over the smoke and pulls it back sharpish. "Cold smoke. That ain't a thing. That ain't a thing, sugar. Uh-uh. Mamma mia."

Go back the way you came, quickly.

a.text:
Ninety trees, and at the ninetieth the paint is fresh.
Beyond it there is no more wood: there is a clearing the shape of a room, floored in ice you can see down into, and under the ice, laid out and neat, a surveyor's kit, a coat, and a pair of boots with the laces still tied.
The blue paint tin is standing on the ice, open, unfrozen.

choices.text: Cut through and bring the kit up.
Take the tin and finish the line.

b.text:
Two feet of snow, then a hatch: a proper one, steel, with a wheel, warm to the hand.
It is a bunker, and it is lit, and there is nobody in it, and the stove in the middle of the main room is burning something that is not wood and is not coal and does not go down as it burns.
b.bubba: "Alright," says Bubba, hands on hips, entirely happy. "Now we're talkin'. Sotto 'a neve, 'nu palazzo."

choices.text: Strip the place of anything useful.
Find out what the stove is burning.

c.text:
You keep a fire and you keep watch, and at some point between three and four in the morning the wood goes quiet in the way it goes quiet when the snow stops.
Something walks the line. It is upright. It stops at each blue mark and puts its hand on it, the way a person counts stairs in the dark, and it is coming this way at exactly the speed of somebody who is not in a hurry.

asides.brave: {member} {steps up front with a weapon ready: "I'll take point."|grins and racks the slide: "Let's see what wants to die today."|is already at the hatch before anyone can argue|steps over the threshold without flinching}
asides.timid: {member} is very still and very quiet and does everything right.
asides.any: {member} {keeps an eye on the sensors and says nothing|watches the approach with a neutral squint|checks their holster with quiet efficiency|stands by the entryway, ready for trouble}

choices.text: Let it come and speak to it.
Put the fire out and {Let it pass|Hold fire and wait|Stay hidden until it moves on|Let it walk by}.

d.text:
You get out, and it takes longer than it took to come in, and the last mile has blue marks on trees you swear you did not pass.
On the road you find the count in your own notebook in your own hand: ninety, then ninety-one, then a mark that is not a number.

a1.text:
The ice does not want to be cut and then, all at once, it does.
The coat pockets hold {paper}, a compass frozen to north whichever way you turn it, and a survey book with the last entry written from underneath the ice, in the same blue.

a2.text:
You take the tin and you paint the ninety-first tree, and the wood makes a sound like a held breath being let go.
The cold breaks. Snow comes off branches for a hundred metres in every direction at once, and the clearing behind you is only a clearing, and the boots under the ice are only boots.
Somebody's work is finished. Something in your pack is heavier than it was.

b1.text:
Tinned food that is still good, forty litres of lamp oil, tools, wire, two coats and a crate of the kind of ammunition nobody stocks any more.
You take what three people can carry uphill through snow, which is less than you would like and more than you should.

b2.text:
You open the door of the stove.
What is in there is not fuel. It is looking back, and it has been burning for a very long time, and it would like the door shut, or opened all the way.

c1.text:
It stops at your fire, puts its hand on the tree beside you as if the tree were the next number, and waits.
You talk. Doesn't, but it turns its head when you get to the part it wants, and when you have got it right it takes something out of the snow at your feet that was not there before and puts it in your hands.

c2.text:
You kill the fire and it goes by close enough to hear it counting, and it counts in a language that stops being a language about halfway along.
In the morning the blue marks are gone off every tree, and the line is still there, worn into the snow, and it goes somewhere you will not be going today.

e_foresttropical.title: {The Canopy|Forty Metres Up And Somebody's Kettle|The Green Room}

n0.text:
Heat like a hand on the back of the neck, and a research platform forty metres up in the canopy with a rope ladder hanging down to head height.
There is a kettle up there. You can hear it. It has been whistling for as long as you have been standing here, and nobody has taken it off.
At the foot of the tree, arranged in a neat square: eleven pairs of boots.
n0.emText:
Heat, green light, a platform forty metres up with a kettle screaming on it, and eleven pairs of boots laid out in a square at the foot of the tree.
The square is deliberate. Somebody made an arrangement here, and the arrangement is still running, and the kettle is the metronome. You are getting quite good at spotting other people's spells. Yours is the one you cannot see.
n0.bubba: Bubba counts the boots twice. "Eleven. Aoh. Eleven pairs an' no feet. Vuo' sape' 'a verita'? I don't like it. Let's go up."

Shout up first.
Cut the ladder down and leave.

a.text:
The platform is boards and mesh and it moves under you. There is a stove, the kettle, eleven camp beds, and a table with a meal laid out on it for eleven, gone bad in the heat, except one plate, which has not.
There is nobody. There is also, quite clearly, somebody: you can hear the platform take weight when you are all standing still.

asides.paranoid: {member} {mutters that someone's definitely watching us from the shadows|checks their six three times and grips their holster|hisses that the signal frequency is rigged|whispers: "They knew we were coming. Look around."}

choices.text: Sit down at the good plate and eat.
Search the platform properly.

b.text:
You lift a pair off the square and the whole canopy above you moves at once, without wind, like an audience leaning in.
The kettle stops. In the silence you can hear something come down the trunk on the far side, fast, and stop, and wait for you to put them back.

choices.text: Put them back and step away.
Keep them.

asides.any: {member} {keeps an eye on the sensors and says nothing|watches the approach with a neutral squint|checks their holster with quiet efficiency|stands by the entryway, ready for trouble}

c.text:
Your voice goes up into the green and does not come back, and about four seconds later somebody up there answers, in your voice, saying the same words, in the same order, with one word changed.
The changed word is a name. It's not a name any of you has heard, and one of you flinches at it anyway.

asides.melancholic: "That was my mother's name," says {member}, very quietly, and then will not discuss it.
asides.any: {member} {keeps an eye on the sensors and says nothing|watches the approach with a neutral squint|checks their holster with quiet efficiency|stands by the entryway, ready for trouble}

choices.text: Answer it. Use the name.
Climb up and see who is doing it.

d.text:
It comes down in a heap of rope and the platform above you does not react at all, which is somehow worse.
Two days later, in {region}, a woman from a university you have never heard of buys your account of it over three coffees and pays for the coffees, and asks you, as you leave, whether the kettle was still going when you cut it.

a1.text:
It is the best meal you have had in a month and it is still hot and it should not be.
Halfway through, the platform takes weight opposite you and the chair moves, and you have the very strong sense of being kept company by somebody being polite about not appearing.
When you finish there is a gift under the plate, in the way there always is when you eat what is offered properly.

a2.text:
Eleven field notebooks, all of them useful, and one of them wrong: the last three weeks are written by a hand that gets better at handwriting each day, the way somebody learns.
You take the eleven, and the mesh floor under the wrong one is worn where something has sat there a great deal.

b1.text:
You put them back in the square, and the canopy relaxes, and the kettle starts again.
On the way out you find a pair of boots on the track that fits one of you exactly. They were not there on the way in. Everybody agrees not to talk about it, and everybody keeps them.

b2.text: The thing that came down the trunk would like them back and it is not going to ask twice.

c1.text:
You say the name into forty metres of green and the wood answers by going completely, absolutely silent: no insects, no birds, no leaf noise.
Into that silence, something comes down to head height and looks at whichever of you flinched, and gives them what it has been holding for eleven people's worth of time.

e_spiritwoods.title: {The Lantern|Somebody Is Walking A Light Between The Trees|Nine Steps Behind}

n0.text:
There is a light in the wood, and it is a lantern, and it is being carried: it swings the way a lamp swings on a person's arm, and it goes behind trunks and comes out the other side.
Whoever is carrying it stays exactly nine steps ahead. When you stop, it stops. When you go back, it comes back with you.
{smell}. Under that, faintly, {smell2}.
n0.emText:
A lantern in the wood, carried, nine steps ahead, matching you.
Everything here is thinner than it is elsewhere: the trees have the quality of a held idea. You know exactly where you are. You are in the part of the world that has not made up its mind, and you woke up in one of these on the first of January and walked out of it alone.
n0.bubba: "Nine steps," says Bubba, counting under his breath. "Nove. Ogni vota nove. That's a fella wit' a system, sugar."

Put your own light out and see what it does.
Call to it. Ask what it wants.
Walk directly at it, fast.

a.text:
An hour, maybe two: the wood does not agree with your watch.
It takes you to a clearing with a well in it, boarded over and weighted with a stone, and it sets the lantern down on the boards, and it is not there any more, and the lantern goes on burning.
Under the boards, something says a word. Once.

b.text:
You put your light out and the wood goes absolutely black except the lantern, which stops, and turns, and comes back three steps.
Then it waits, at six, which is the closest it has been, and holds itself a little higher, the way somebody holds a light up to see a face.

c.text:
"Nine," it says. Not a voice: the number arrives in the same way a smell arrives.
"Nine," it says again, and the lantern swings, and you understand that it is not telling you the distance. It is telling you the price, and it is waiting to hear what you are counting in.

choices.text: Offer nine days.
Offer nine of something else.
Offer it nothing and say so plainly.

asides.hedonistic: {member} offers nine drinks. Doesn't laugh. Neither does anybody else.
asides.disciplined: {member} {follows standard breach protocol by the book|clears every corner with military precision|keeps a steady firing stance and monitors the sensors|checks the ammo count and maintains position}
