d.text:
You cover nine steps and it does not move, and at the end of the nine you are standing in front of a lantern hanging in the air at the height of a hand, with nothing holding it, in a wood that has gone completely still.
Then the lantern goes out, and everything that was standing nine steps behind you all afternoon is now standing directly in front of you, in the dark.

a1.text:
The stone comes off, and the boards come up, and the well is dry, and there is a ladder, and at the bottom of the ladder there is a room that is older than the well, with the wood's own name written round the walls about four hundred times.
What is in the middle of the room has been waiting to be given to somebody who came the whole way at nine steps and did not rush it.

a2.text:
It burns for eleven days in your pack without oil and then stops, and after that it is a lantern.
While it burns, nothing follows you at night, which you only notice properly on the twelfth day.

a3.text:
You answer it, and you get it right, which is largely luck and a little bit of listening.
The boards do not move. The word is said again, gently, and this time it is a thank you, and the wood opens a way out that is about a fifth as long as the way in.
On the path there is {relicWord}, put down where you will trip over it, because it has never had to give anybody anything before and it is not sure how.

b1.text:
It comes to arm's length and looks at each of you for as long as it takes, and at one of you for longer.
Then it puts the lantern in that person's hand, closes their fingers on the handle, and is not there, and the wood is an ordinary wood full of ordinary night.

c1.text:
Nine days go somewhere. You are not aware of losing them; the calendar is.
What you have when you come out of the wood is nine days older, nine days poorer, and holding something that is worth a great deal more than nine days.

c2.text:
Nine coins, nine steps, nine words, nine of anything: it takes what is offered, if it is offered in nines, which is the only rule it has ever had.
What it gives back is not what you asked for and is worth having anyway.

c3.text:
"Nothing," you say. "We have nothing for you and we are not going to pretend otherwise."
The lantern goes down, and stays down, and burns on the ground where it was set, and the wood lets you out in the direction you actually wanted rather than the direction it was taking you.
Honesty is not always paid. It is, however, always noticed.

e_mountain.title: {The Cairn|Somebody Comes Up Here Every Week|The Offering At The Col}

n0.text:
Three hundred metres above the last house in {country}, at the col, there is a cairn with things left on it.
Not flowers. On the top stone, in a row: {offering}, {offering2}, and a third that somebody has taken away and left the mark of.
The stones are dry. It rained here two hours ago.
n0.emText:
A cairn at the col with things left on it: {offering}, {offering2}, and the dry ring where a third stood until recently.
The stones are dry in weather that has soaked you to the shoulders. Something up here is holding a small patch of the world exempt, and doing it politely, and doing it every week.
n0.bubba: Bubba sets his hat on the stone next to the rest of it, thinks better of it, takes it back. "Nah. You don't leave nothin' at a table you ain't ate at. 'A regola e' chesta."

Wait for whoever brings these up.
Take the cairn apart.
Follow the path the offerings come up.

a.text:
You put something of yours on the stone, and the weather changes: not dramatically, just a wind that had been in your face all morning and now is not.
Going down, you find the way easier than it was coming up, which is not how mountains work, and at the last gate somebody has left {payment} on the post with a stone on top of it so the wind cannot have it.

b.text:
Two hours in the lee of a rock, and then {stranger} comes up the last of the path with a carrier bag and stops dead when they see you.
"You've not moved anything," they say. It is the first thing they check, and they check it properly, on their knees, before they will look at you again.

c.text:
The stones come down easily. Under the bottom one there is a hollow lined with slate, and in the hollow there is a small heavy thing wrapped in oilcloth, and taking it is the easiest theft any of you have ever committed.
The wind gets up while you are doing it. The path down is not where you left it.

"For the col," they say, as if that were the whole answer, and then, because you have waited two hours in the wet: "For what walks it. It has been walked a long time and it does not like being walked on for nothing."
They teach you the four things you leave and the one thing you never leave, and make you say the one thing back.

b2.text:
They look at you for a long moment and then hand you the bag, and it is much heavier than a bag of small objects should be.
You do it for a month. On the fourth week the col leaves something for you, which is not how the arrangement has ever run, and the woman at the farm goes white when she sees it.

d1.text:
The job is to go up in weather she cannot go up in and put a specific thing on a specific stone at a specific hour, and to not look behind you between the col and the second gate.
You do it. You do not look. What is behind you talks the whole way down, pleasantly, about people you have never met, and knows all their names, and one of them is yours.

d2.text:
"Ninety-one," she says. "Ninety-one and then the col comes down here and does the asking itself. It did it in {timeAgo} and there is nothing left of the house it asked at but the gate."
She pays you to make the week's climb once, which is all you are willing to promise, and pays over the odds for it.

e_mountainice.title: {The Crevasse|Forty Metres Down And Still Talking|The Rope Somebody Left}

n0.text:
A rope, anchored properly, ice screws in sound ice, going down into a crevasse and pulled tight.
Someone's on the other end of it. Somebody has been on the other end of it for a while, judging by the ice that has formed on the rope where it crosses the lip.
When you get to the edge and look, a voice comes up from a long way down, conversational, unhurried, and says: "Is that you, then?"
n0.emText:
A rope going down into a crevasse, tight, iced over at the lip. Down there, a voice, unhurried: "Is that you, then?"
You have never heard the voice. It knows you. That is now the fourth thing this month that has known you when you did not know it, and you are keeping count, because counting is the only archive you have.
n0.bubba: Bubba lies flat and shouts down the hole. "WHO'S ASKIN'?" A pause. "He says he knows ya, sugar. Uh-uh. Nun me piace."

Forty metres down the blue goes very dark and then opens: a chamber in the ice with a shelf of gear on it, twenty years of it, arranged.
The man on the end of the rope is sitting on the shelf. He is not cold. He offers you the thermos. He has been down here since a date he gives cheerfully and which is on the wrong side of what a person survives.

c.text:
It comes up light, and it keeps coming, and it keeps coming: a hundred and ten metres of rope out of a crevasse that is sixty deep, and on the end of it a harness, buckled, with nobody in it and no wear on the leg loops.
The voice, still down there, says: "Ah. Well."

d.text:
You cut it, and the end goes down without a sound, and the voice does not shout.
It says, quite kindly, "That's all right," and then nothing at all, and the crevasse is a hole in a glacier on a cold afternoon.
One of your party does not sleep properly for a fortnight and will not say which part of it is the problem.

a1.text:
He comes up easily. He weighs about as much as a coat.
At the lip, in daylight, he thanks each of you by name, walks eleven paces onto the snow, and is not there. The gear you brought up with him is entirely real and worth a fortune to the right museum.

a2.text:
Forty years of mountaineering hardware, all of it good, some of it made by firms that closed before you were born.
He helps you pack it and holds the rope while you go up, which is the part that stays with you.

a3.text:
"The rest of the rope," he says.
Then he explains, patiently, what he means, and it takes some time, and by the end of it you are quite certain that the ice has been keeping him not out of kindness but out of an agreement, and that you have been handed the terms.

b1.text:
"The second one," he says. "There's always a second one on a rope. I keep listening for the second one."
Zero second anchor. There never was. What comes up the rope when you finally stop talking is not him.

b2.text:
You promise, and you mean it, and the rescue service in {region} takes the grid reference and looks at each other in a way you will think about later.
They have that reference. They have had it for a long time. They pay your expenses, take a statement, and ask you, very carefully, whether he used your names.

e_mountaindesert.title: {The Stair|Two Hundred Steps Cut Into Nothing|The Ladder In The Rock}

n0.text:
Steps cut into the rock face, going up: two hundred of them, worn in the middle, ending at a ledge with nothing on it and nowhere to go.
No temple. No door. No niche. A ledge, an arm's length deep, two hundred steps above the valley floor, and worn steps mean feet, and a lot of them.
At the bottom, in the shade, somebody has left a water jar. It is full.
n0.emText:
Two hundred steps cut into a cliff, worn hollow in the middle, and at the top a ledge with nothing on it at all.
Something used to be there. You are becoming an expert on the shape of things that used to be there. At the bottom of the stair, in the shade, a full water jar, put down today by somebody who expects the walk to be made.
n0.bubba: Bubba drinks from the jar, which everyone would have advised against. "Ah. Fresh. Somebody's mindin' this place. Statte accuorto ncoppa, sugar."

When you have been there long enough for your breathing to settle, the rock behind your shoulders is warm, and there is a hollow in it at the height of a head, worn by heads.

"It's my week," he says. "You have to keep it full. If it's empty they come down."
He says this the way you would say that the bins go out on Tuesday.

c.text: Two hundred steps of dropped things: coins from six centuries, buttons, a shoe, four rings, a knife with a saint's name on the blade, and, half under a slab, in {relicWord}, something that was not dropped but hidden.

d.text:
At night the steps are cold and the ledge is not.
Standing on it in the dark, you can see the valley the way it was: lights in a pattern of a town that is not there, and a road going somewhere that has not existed in four hundred years, and, on the ledge with you, the shoulder-to-shoulder press of a queue.
Nobody pushes. You are, however, in the way.

a1.text: Leaning against the warm rock, you get a sudden sharp clarity: four minutes of knowing exactly where you are, in a sense of the word 'where' that includes the year, and coming out of it you can feel the size of the mistake you have been making about something.

a2.text:
You come down without mentioning it and somebody at the bottom takes one look at your face and hands you the water jar without a word.
Whatever the ledge does, it does not do it to everybody, and the people who keep the jar full have known that for four hundred years.

b1.text:
"The ones on the stair," he says, and then will not be drawn further, except to say that his grandmother saw them and that they {Walk in|Step through the entrance|Cross the threshold|Head inside} a queue and that you must never be on the steps when they are, because there is only one width of stair.
He tells you when, which is the useful part, and it is tonight.

b2.text:
You tip it out on the stones and the boy goes white and runs, which is the correct response, and which you will remember.
They come down. There is only one width of stair, and you are on it.

b3.text:
You fill both jars and carry them up to the second landing where they are supposed to sit, and the boy talks the whole way about a bicycle he is saving for.
At the bottom his mother is waiting with the whole family, who knew you were coming before you did, and who feed you until you cannot stand.

n0.text:

The paint is Collective. The plates are four different countries. The tyres are perfect.
The heat is still coming up out of the ground and the metal is cold.
n0.emText:
Eleven lorry cabs in a line under a moved dune, doors open, tyres perfect, metal cold in a desert.
The whole convoy is holding its breath and has been for years. You know that state. It is the state you woke up in: everything preserved, nothing explained, and the doors open as though whoever left did it in a hurry that has since become permanent.

a2.text:

b1.text:
You drive out with ten engines idling behind you and they are still idling when the dune closes the mirror.
It is a good lorry. It is worth real money. For a year afterwards it will not start for anybody but whoever turned that key.

b2.text:

What happened to eleven drivers happened over about four seconds. You get the four seconds. You also get what they dropped when it happened.

d2.text:
A metre down: sand, then a floor. Tiled. Warm.
A metre further along, a hatch, and the hatch has been opened from underneath eleven times by eleven pairs of hands, and never opened from the top by anybody.

e_badlands.title: {The Bone Bed|Everything Here Died Facing The Same Way|The Wash Below The Rim}

n0.text:
A flash flood has cut a new channel and opened a bone bed in the side of it: hundreds of animals, layered, and every skull turned the same way.
Half of them are species that should not be in the same century as each other. All of them are facing the rim of the canyon, where there is a gap in the rock like a doorway with nothing behind it.
{smell}, and under your boots the ground is warm.
n0.emText:
A new channel cut by a flood, and in its wall a bone bed: hundreds of animals from centuries that should not touch, all of them facing the same gap in the rim.
They were all looking at the same thing when it happened to them. You have never been able to find out what you were looking at.
n0.bubba: Bubba crouches at the layer line with his hat pushed back. "That's a whole lotta critters agreein' on somethin'. Uh-huh. E nun era 'na bella cosa."

The museum in {region} is delighted, pays well, and asks for the location, which you give. Four months later there is no bone bed: there is a fence, a Foundation seal, and a man on a folding chair who has been told your name.

d.text:
After dark the warm ground gets warmer and the bones in the wall do not move, which is important, because everything else does: your shadows, thrown by the fire, go the wrong way and lie flat against the bone bed and stay there when you stand up.
At some point in the small hours the whole herd, all of it, all the layers at once, turns to face the rim again, with a sound like a book being shut.

a1.text:
The same country, the same hour, and no bone bed in the wash: the wall is clean rock, uncut, unflooded.
You are through for about ninety seconds before the doorway behind you starts to close, and you get back with everybody, and one of you is carrying something that was picked up on the other side and which does not exist on this one.

One of them is holding the tin box. The photograph is older than photography.

b2.text:
Layer nine is worked stone, laid, with a floor and a drain and a doorway of its own, and the animals above it are not a bone bed at all.
They are a roof.

choices.text: Dig the cable up.
Stop the generator.

a1.text:
You are eleven kilometres away when somebody uses the name on the wallet to call across the tundra, once, clearly, in a voice that carries the way voices do not.
The wallet has three hundred in it and a card that is worth more than three hundred to the right office. The photograph you keep. In four months you will look at it again.

a2.text:
You sit down in a portable toilet in the middle of the tundra with the door open, because you are the kind of person who follows a thing through.
What you get, over about four minutes, is the whole project: what is going to be built here, who is paying, what is under the grid that they want to be on top of, and why they brought a chair.

b1.text:
It comes up two metres long, sharpened, iron, and old: older than the survey, older than the project number, older than the orange paint by centuries.
It was here first. The survey grid is centred on it because whoever laid the grid found it and built the whole job round it, and the eight piles are somebody's attempt to keep it in the ground.

b2.text:
You build a ninth pile at the centre, over the flush stake, and sit down, and nothing happens for two hours.
Then the moss closes over your pile, and over all eight, and the dead circle greens in front of you at the speed of a tide coming in, and the survey stakes at the edge of the grid fall over, all of them, in one long clatter going round.

d1.text:
It goes down four metres and ends in a plate, and the plate is bolted to something that is not a rock.
What you get out of it before the generator stops on its own is a coil of cable, a plate of an alloy that does not belong to this decade, and a very strong sense of having interrupted something halfway.

d2.text:
You kill it, and the silence is enormous, and every stake in the grid ninety minutes behind you goes over at once. You hear it. Across ninety minutes of tundra, you hear it.
When you get back the moss has closed and the portable toilet is gone and the wheelbarrow has both its wheels.

e_permafrost.title: {The Thaw|What The Ground Is Giving Back|Fourteen Metres Of Held Breath}

n0.text:
The ground is going soft for the first time in eleven thousand years and it is giving things back.
A post, upright, worked with a blade. A boat, or the ribs of one, a hundred kilometres from water. And a hand: a human hand, brown, perfect, at the end of an arm that is still in the ice, and the fingers are closed on something.
The smell is not decay. It is more like {smell}.
n0.emText:
Eleven thousand years of held ground going soft, and everything it has been holding coming up at once: a carved post, the ribs of a boat, and a hand out of the ice with its fingers shut on something.
The ground here has better memory than you do and it is losing it in a single season, and you can feel exactly how that feels from the inside.
n0.bubba: Bubba takes his hat off to the hand, seriously, no joke in it. "Signo'. Requiem. Awright. Now let's see what he's holdin'."

choices.text: Open the hand.
Dig the arm out. Get all of him.
Follow the strip of thaw.
Take the post. It is the only thing you can carry.

a.text:
The fingers give like cold wax, one at a time, and what is in the palm is a bead of something dark that is warm, and that gets warmer the longer it is out of the ice.
Behind you, the thaw accelerates. You can hear it: water moving under a metre of ground for a hundred metres in every direction.

choices.text: Keep the bead.
Put it back and close the hand.

asides.any: {member} {keeps an eye on the sensors and says nothing|watches the approach with a neutral squint|checks their holster with quiet efficiency|stands by the entryway, ready for trouble}

b.text:
Six hours with picks and hot water and he comes up entire: a man of about thirty, dressed for weather, with a healed break in his forearm and four objects on him.
The fourth object is not of his century, or ours. It was in his coat, and his coat was made to hold it, and the coat is eleven thousand years old.

c.text:
The thaw runs in a strip two metres wide for four kilometres and ends at a mound, and the mound is not thawing at all: it is white with frost in the middle of a warm afternoon.
There is a door in it. There has always been a door in it. The thaw came from the door outwards, like something breathing on the ground.

choices.text: Open the door.
Put your ear to it first.

d.text:
It takes two of you to carry and it is worth every step.
The university in {region} pays out of a fund that exists for exactly this, and a woman from the Foundation is at the loading bay when you deliver it, and buys you a coffee, and asks four questions about what else was in the strip.

a1.text:
It is warm in your pack all the way home and it never cools.
Doesn't do anything else. That is the point: it does not do anything else, and eleven thousand years ago a man walked into a cold he could not survive rather than put it down.

a2.text:
You put it back and fold the fingers over it and pack the ice round the hand with your own hands until it is covered.
The thaw stops. Not slows: stops, in a ring around him, and the water that was running under the ground goes quiet.
What you take away is what was under the boat ribs, which the ground offers up while you are washing your hands.

c1.text:
It opens outwards, which is wrong for a mound, and the cold that comes out of it is not a temperature, it is a weight.
Inside there is a stair, and at the bottom of the stair there is a room with eleven thousand years of quiet in it and something in the middle of the quiet that has been waiting for the ground to soften.

c2.text:
Breathing. Slow: about one to your four. And under the breathing, a sound like somebody turning over in bed.
You back off, and you mark the mound on the map, and you take the news to the one office that will do anything with it, and they thank you in a way that suggests they knew, and pay you in a way that suggests they did not know it had started.

e_volcano.title: {The Vent|A Man Explaining That Lava Is Safe Now|Four Hundred Degrees And A Deckchair}

n0.text:
There is a deckchair at the lip of an active vent, and a man in it, in shorts, reading a newspaper, at a distance where the newspaper should be alight.
He has a cool box. He offers you a drink without looking up.
"It's been safe since the ritual," he says. "Nobody believes me. There's a radio programme about it."
n0.emText:
A deckchair at the lip of an active vent, and a man in it in shorts, reading, at a temperature that should have taken the paper off him.
"It's been safe since the ritual," he says. Since the ritual. That is your calendar he is using. Everything in this world dates itself from the night they took ninety-two per cent of you and made a spear out of it.
n0.bubba: Bubba is already in the second deckchair with a bottle from the man's cool box. "He's right, y'know. It's warm. It's real warm. Ma nun coce. Sit down, sugar."

choices.text: Sit down and have the drink.
Ask what happened during the ritual.
Go down into the vent.
Tell him to get away from the edge and mean it.

a.text:
You sit at the lip of a volcano in a deckchair and drink something cold, and the heat comes up past you and does not touch you, and it is the strangest twenty minutes of the season.
He talks. He has been doing this for four years. His wife thinks he is at work.

choices.text: Ask what he does down there.
Stay until dark.

asides.any: {member} {keeps an eye on the sensors and says nothing|watches the approach with a neutral squint|checks their holster with quiet efficiency|stands by the entryway, ready for trouble}

b.text:
"Something came up and something went down," he says. "The mountain got quiet after. Not cold. Quiet."
He was here. He was one of the men on the emergency cordon on the thirty-first, and he has the photographs, and he keeps them in the cool box under the bottles, in a plastic bag, because that is where they are safest.

choices.text: Look at the photographs.
Buy the photographs.

c.text:
There are steps. Somebody cut steps.
Forty metres down it is bright and it is bearable and the air is wrong in the mouth, and there is a ledge, and on the ledge there are things left: tools, a boot, a wedding ring, a Foundation seal with the date scratched off, and a doorway in the rock with the heat going into it.

choices.text: Go through the doorway.
Take what is on the ledge and climb out.

asides.any: {member} {keeps an eye on the sensors and says nothing|watches the approach with a neutral squint|checks their holster with quiet efficiency|stands by the entryway, ready for trouble}

d.text:
He goes, because you said it like that, and he is furious about it, and halfway up the slope he stops being furious and starts shaking.
The safe zone ends four metres from where his deckchair was. You find that out by watching what happens to the deckchair when he takes it.

a1.text:
"Fetching," he says. "Fetching. There's a ledge. People leave things and other people want them."
He is a courier for a doorway in a volcano and he is paid in cash by four different offices. He will take you down as far as the ledge and no further, and he tells you exactly why not, and the reason is not fire.

a2.text:
After dark the vent glow lights him from underneath like a stage, and the mountain does something you will never be able to describe to anybody: it exhales, once, and the exhalation is shaped, and there are words in it that are not in any language and are unmistakably a greeting.
He waves back. He does it the way you wave at a neighbour.

b1.text:
Four photographs of the night of the thirty-first, taken from a cordon at the wrong angle, of a thing going down into a vent that is a great deal larger than the vent.
The fourth photograph has people in it. One of them is looking at the camera.
b1.emText:
Four photographs from the cordon on the thirty-first of December, 2001. Something enormous going down into a vent that is far too small for it.
In the fourth, at the edge of the frame, there is a woman on a stretcher with her eyes open, and you have never seen your own face from the outside on that night, and now you have.
b1.bubba: Bubba looks at the fourth one for a long time and then puts it face down. "Nah, sugar. Basta accussi'. Not today."

b2.text:
He will not sell them. He gives you one, the second, which is the least useful and the most beautiful, and asks you to show it to people.
You do. Four people laugh. The fifth pays enough to keep the whole party fed for a month and asks where the other three are.

c1.text:
Through the doorway the heat stops entirely, which the body reads as falling.
What is on the other side has been paid by everybody who has ever stood on that ledge and it is very interested in somebody who came through without leaving anything.

c2.text:
Tools, a boot, a ring and a seal. The ring is gold and the seal is worth four times the gold to the right buyer.
On the way up the steps you understand that you have taken payment off an altar, and that this is noted, and that it is not the sort of debt that gets collected quickly.

e_ruins.title: {The Sunken Floor|A Room That Is Lower Than It Was|The House With Four Cellars}

n0.text:
Half a house, and the half that is left has a floor in it that has gone down: not collapsed, lowered, all in one piece, tiles unbroken, about a metre and a half below where the doorstep says it should be.
At the far side of the sunken floor there is a door that used to be a cellar door and is now at eye level, and it is shut, and it is newer than the house.
In the wallpaper, {sign}.
n0.emText:
Half a house with its floor lowered a metre and a half, all in one piece, tiles unbroken, and a cellar door that is now at eye level and is newer than everything around it.
Something took a level of this building away and put a different one in. You know the trick from the inside. There is an entire floor of you missing and the door to it is at the wrong height too.
n0.bubba: Bubba drops down onto the tiles and stamps twice. "Solid. Uh-huh. Somebody built this here on a Tuesday, sugar, an' the house ain't from a Tuesday."

choices.text: Open the cellar door.
Take the floor up.
Search the standing half of the house.
Knock. Properly. And wait.

a.text:
Behind it: a corridor, dry, plastered, lit by nothing you can identify, running further than the footprint of the house allows.
On the left-hand wall, at regular intervals, are doors, and each door has a number, and the numbers do not run in order, and the fourth one is your own house number, whichever of you is thinking about that.

choices.text: Open the numbered door that means something to somebody.
Walk the corridor to the end.

asides.nervous: {member} {sweats inside their helmet and asks how much air we have left|keeps looking back toward the lander with wide eyes|jumps at every creak in the hull|wonders aloud if we can just leave right now}

b.text:
The tiles come up in one piece each, laid on sand, and under the sand there is a second floor, and it is the original, and between the two there is a hand's width of space with things in it: a shoe, a comb, {paper}, a bundle of letters, a doll.
Everything that was on the old floor when it was lowered was swept into the gap first. Neatly.

c.text:
Two rooms and a stair to nowhere.
In the second room there is a table with a meal on it, four places, cutlery down, and a chair pulled out. The food is dust. The chair is not: the chair has been sat in this week, and the dust round it has been disturbed by a coat.

choices.text: Sit in the chair.
Lay a fifth place.

d.text:
You knock on a cellar door at eye level in a ruined house and you wait, and it takes a minute and a half, and then somebody knocks back: four knocks, evenly spaced, from a long way off, getting nearer with each one.
The fourth is on the other side of the door.

choices.text: Open it.
Say who you are through the door.

a1.text:
It opens on a room you know, and it is not this decade, and there are people in it who are not surprised to see you and do not stop what they are doing.
You are in there for four minutes. You come out with something that was on the sideboard, and with a headache, and a certainty about a thing you had chosen not to be certain about.

a2.text:
Four hundred metres, which the house does not have.
The end of the corridor is a wall with a bell push in it. Zero bell, there is no wire, and when you press it, somewhere behind you, in the ruin, a door opens.

c1.text:
The chair is warm. From the chair, the table looks laid rather than abandoned, and the room looks lit, and there is a fifth person in the doorway you cannot look at directly.
You are welcome. You are, quite clearly and quite kindly, welcome, and you are not being asked for anything, and that is the frightening part.

c2.text:
You set a fifth place with what is in the sideboard and you sit down and eat your own food at a dead table.
When you have finished, the fifth place has been used. Nobody saw it happen. Under the plate there is {relicWord} and a note in a hand nobody can read, and the pulled-out chair is pushed in.

d1.text:
The corridor is there and so is the person who knocked, and they are a metre and a half below you, standing in the old house at the old floor level, looking up.
They have been down there since the floor was put in. They are not asking to come out. They are asking whether it is still {timeAgo} up here.

d2.text:
You say your name and your business through a cellar door.
The answer comes back in your own voice, saying your name and your business, and then a second voice, saying: "Not that one. The other one. Send the other one."
Nobody opens the door. Everybody agrees, later, that this was correct.

e_graveyard.title: {The Fresh Grave|Nobody Has Died Here Since {timeAgo}|Dug Last Night}

n0.text:
A country graveyard with nine hundred years in it and one grave dug last night: sharp edges, heaped spoil, no stone, no flowers, no notice on the gate.
The parish register in the porch says nobody has been buried here since {timeAgo}.
The hole is exactly the right size, and it is dug the way a professional digs, and there is a spade left in the spoil heap, which no professional would ever do.
n0.emText:
One fresh grave in a nine-hundred-year churchyard, cut last night by somebody who knew the work, and a spade left standing in the spoil, which nobody who knows the work would do.
The hole is the right size for a person. You have a horrible and specific feeling about which person, and it is the same feeling you get looking at a doorway you cannot remember walking through.
n0.bubba: Bubba looks in the hole, then at you, then back in the hole. "Sugar, that's about your size. Nun me piace pe' niente. C'mon now."

choices.text: Get in the grave.
Wait for whoever comes back for the spade.
Fill it in.
Find the priest.

a.text:
It is deep enough that the sky is a rectangle and the church is gone.
The sides are cut clean. At the foot end, at about the depth of a knee, there is a niche cut into the earth, and there is something in the niche, wrapped, and it is the only reason this hole exists.

b.text:
They come back at dusk: a woman in her fifties with a wheelbarrow and a second spade, and she is not a gravedigger, she is a solicitor from {region}, and she has been digging her own family's graves for two years because the parish will not.
"There's nobody in any of them," she says. "That's the thing nobody will put in writing."

choices.text: Help her dig.
Ask what she is expecting to find.

asides.empathetic: {member} {looks at the wreckage and shakes their head: "Tough way to go."|checks for survivor logs with a quiet sigh|hopes whoever was here got out in time|mutters a quiet condolence for the crew}
asides.any: {member} {keeps an eye on the sensors and says nothing|watches the approach with a neutral squint|checks their holster with quiet efficiency|stands by the entryway, ready for trouble}

c.text:
It takes forty minutes and it is the right thing to do and everybody knows it.
At about the halfway point the spoil stops going in. It goes in and it is not there; the level does not rise. You are shovelling earth into a hole that is not accepting it, and the last of the light is going.

choices.text: {Keep going|Push deeper|Continue forward|Press on} until it is full.
Stop, and put the spade back where it was.

d.text:
The priest is in the vestry with the register pages in front of him, the four that were cut out, and a glass of something, and he is not surprised.
"It's the fourteenth," he says. "They dig one every so often and if you fill it in they dig another and if you leave it alone it fills itself and there is nothing in the rite for this, I have looked, I have written to the diocese."

choices.text: Ask what happened with the first thirteen.
Offer to sit up with the grave all night.

asides.nurturing: {member} takes the glass off him gently and puts the kettle on instead.
asides.any: {member} {keeps an eye on the sensors and says nothing|watches the approach with a neutral squint|checks their holster with quiet efficiency|stands by the entryway, ready for trouble}

b1.text:
Two hours in the dark with a solicitor, opening a grave that is a hundred years old, and she is right: there is a coffin, and it is empty, and it has been empty since it went in, because the wood has never been under weight.
What is in it instead is a box of papers, and the papers are what her family has been paying for the silence of for a century.

b2.text:
"Nothing," she says. "That's what I'm expecting. I want to be able to say I've seen the nothing."
You sit with her until the light is gone and she talks about her brother, and at the end of it she gives you the second spade and {payment}, and drives home, and does not dig again.

c1.text:
You fill a hole that will not fill, in the dark, until the spoil heap is gone and the hole is exactly as deep as it was.
Then something takes hold of the spade from the other end and does not pull, just holds, the way somebody holds a door you are trying to shut.

c2.text:
You stop, and you put the spade back in the spoil at exactly the angle you found it, and you leave the churchyard by the gate rather than the wall.
In the morning the grave is filled and the turf is on and the grass has taken, and the sexton, who has not been out in a year, will not discuss it.

d1.text:
"Filled, dug, filled, dug, and after the ninth I stopped filling them."
The five he stopped filling are all in the north corner, all grassed over, all with grass a different green, and the priest has never once been able to bring himself to walk on it.
You walk on it. Something under it is very glad somebody finally did.

d2.text:
You sit up in a churchyard from dark to four with a flask and a priest who talks for the first two hours and sleeps for the last two.
At four the grave fills itself. It takes about a minute and it does it from the bottom, and there is a sound with it that is nearly a voice, and afterwards there is a stone that was not there, with a name on it, and the name is not anybody's yet.

e_swamp.title: {The Chapel In The Water|Ankle Deep In Somebody's Nave|The Roof Is Still Above The Reeds}

n0.text:
The reeds part on a chapel roof. The rest of it is under, and the water is exactly waist deep in the doorway and stays waist deep all the way to the altar, which is not how water works in a building that is standing on a slope.
Candles have been lit in there. Recently. On a shelf above the waterline there are four, and two are still burning, and there is no way in but the way you came.
n0.emText:
A chapel drowned to the roofline, the water exactly waist deep all the way to the altar regardless of the floor, and four candles on a shelf above the line with two of them still lit.
Somebody comes here and keeps a rule. Rules like that hold a place together the way a stitch holds a wound. You have about eight per cent of yourself and no stitches at all.
n0.bubba: Bubba wades in first, hat held up over his head like a man carrying a cake. "Aoh. Nun sta' fredda. Sugar, this water ain't cold. It oughta be cold."

choices.text: Wade to the altar.
Wait outside for whoever lights the candles.
Go down. Look at the floor.
Take the candles and go.

a.text:
The altar is above the water by the thickness of a hand. On it: a bowl, a stone, and a photograph of a man in a suit that fitted him ten years ago, weighted down with a coin.
Under the water, all round the altar step, the floor is covered in coins. Thousands. Every one of them face up.

choices.text: Take a coin.
Add a coin.
Take the photograph.

asides.hedonistic: {member} is doing arithmetic about thousands of coins and not enjoying anybody's reaction.
asides.any: {member} {keeps an eye on the sensors and says nothing|watches the approach with a neutral squint|checks their holster with quiet efficiency|stands by the entryway, ready for trouble}

b.text:
A woman comes at dusk in waders with four candles in a bread bag, and she does the whole thing without speaking: in, light, out, and on the way out she puts one hand flat on the door frame.
She has done this every week for eleven years. She was told to by somebody who is in the photograph on the altar.

choices.text: Ask her to teach you the rule.
Offer to take a week for her.

c.text:
You go under. The water is warm and clear and there is light from somewhere below.
The floor is a foot below your feet and it is tiled and it is dry: there is a skin on the underside of the water, and under the skin the chapel is a dry chapel with pews and a hymn board with numbers still on it, and somebody is sitting in the third row from the back.

d.text:
You take four candles out of a chapel, two of them burning, and the water follows you.
Not fast. It comes out of the door behind you at walking pace, keeps to waist height, and stays exactly with you for two kilometres through a swamp until somebody has the sense to put the candles down on a tussock.

a1.text:
The coin is silver and old and worth something, and taking it turns every other coin on that floor face down.
All of them. At once. With a sound like a very long word being said backwards.

a2.text:
You put your own coin on the altar face up and the water drops, all at once, by the width of a hand, all through the chapel.
On the floor by the altar step, uncovered, is {relicWord} that has been under water for a long time and is completely dry.

a3.text:
The photograph is dry and the coin holding it down is not.
When you lift it, the man in the suit that fitted him ten years ago is standing at the back of the chapel, waist deep, waiting to be asked something. He has been waiting eleven years and he is extremely patient.

b1.text:
She teaches you the rule, which is four candles, one hand on the frame, and nothing said inside.
Then she tells you what happens when a week is missed, which happened once, in the second year, and which is why the village on the other side of the reeds has forty houses and thirty-one roofs.

b2.text:
You take a week. It is four candles and eleven kilometres and a wet afternoon.
On the way out, with your hand flat on the door frame, something puts its hand flat on the other side of the frame, level with yours, the way children do at a window.
She is waiting at the reed edge. "It's never done that," she says, and then she gives you the bread bag, which means the job is yours whenever you want it.

e_temple.title: {The Offering|Somebody Still Feeds This Place|Four Bowls And One Empty}

n0.text:
The temple is roofless and the steps are worn and there are four bowls on the threshold with food in them, fresh, and a fifth bowl that is empty and clean and set apart.
The food in the four is untouched. The empty one has been used, and washed, and put back, today.
{smell}, and from inside, {sound}.
n0.emText:
Four bowls of fresh food on a roofless threshold, untouched, and a fifth bowl, empty, washed, set apart.
The fifth is the one that is being eaten out of. Whatever lives here has a diet and it is not the food. You have opinions about beings that take something other than what is offered. You have been the something other.
n0.bubba: "Four full, one empty," says Bubba, counting on his fingers like it needs counting. "Vide 'a chesta. Somebody's hungry an' it ain't for rice."

Go inside.
Eat from one of the four.
Wait for whoever brings the food.

a.text:
Whatever you put in it is gone before you have straightened up. Not taken: gone, in the way a word is gone once said.
The fifth bowl is clean again. And on the step beside it there is now something that was not there, put down the way you put down change on a counter.

choices.text: Take it.
Put something else in the bowl and see how long it goes on.

b.text:
Roofless, floored in grass, and at the far end a plinth with nothing on it and the marks where the something stood.
It was taken out through the wall rather than the door: you can see where the stone was opened and put back, and put back by somebody who could not quite match the courses.

choices.text: Open the wall again.
Stand on the plinth.

asides.artistic: {member} finds paint in the shelter of the plinth: colours nobody has been able to make for a thousand years.
asides.any: {member} {keeps an eye on the sensors and says nothing|watches the approach with a neutral squint|checks their holster with quiet efficiency|stands by the entryway, ready for trouble}

c.text:
It is very good and it is very plain and it is warm, and the moment it is swallowed every bird within a mile leaves at once.
What comes to the threshold is not angry. It is confused, and it is looking for the fifth thing, and it is going to keep looking with its hands.

d.text:
It is a boy on a moped with a crate on the back, and he does the four bowls in ninety seconds and takes the fifth one down to the stream and washes it and puts it back.
"It's a job," he says. "It pays. My aunt did it. You want it? I'm going to {region} in the autumn and somebody has to."

choices.text: Take the job for a season.
Ask what happens if the fifth bowl is not washed.

a1.text: It is small and heavy and it is warm on one face, and it has been given rather than found, which is a distinction that matters enormously to certain buyers and to certain other things.

a2.text:
Eleven times. You put in eleven things, of decreasing value, and every one of them is taken, and on the eleventh the exchange stops being an exchange.
What is put down on the step the eleventh time is not payment. It is a request, and it is written in the only alphabet everybody understands, which is a map.

b1.text:
The wall comes out in four courses and behind it there is a cavity with a wooden crate in it, banded, stamped with a Foundation seal and a date, and never collected.
Whoever took the temple's god away hid it here to come back for and did not come back.

b2.text:
You stand where a god stood and nothing happens for about ninety seconds.
Then the roof is on. Only from the inside, only while you are standing there, and it is painted, and it is beautiful, and there are four hundred people in the nave who are extremely pleased to see you and have been waiting a long time and are very sorry about what comes next.

d1.text:
Four bowls a day for a season, and the fifth washed in the stream, and by the third week you are doing it without thinking, and by the sixth you are talking to it.
On the last day of the season it answers, briefly, and gives you something for your trouble, and the boy in {region} gets a letter about it that he will never show anybody.

d2.text:
"It got missed in the bad winter," he says. "Two days. My aunt's hands were bad."
What he describes took four days to stop and cost the village its orchard, and he says it in the tone of a boy describing a power cut, and then he gets back on the moped and asks if you want a lift down.

e_castle.title: {The Postern|The Small Door At The Back|Somebody Uses This Gate}

n0.text:
The castle is a ruin and a ticket office and a car park, and round the back, behind the interpretation boards, there is a postern gate that is not on the plan on the board.
It is oiled. The step in front of it is worn and swept. There is a bootscraper.
The main gate takes four euros. This one takes something else.
n0.emText:
A ruin with a ticket office at the front and, round the back behind the boards, a postern that is not on the plan: oiled hinges, swept step, a bootscraper.
The castle is a museum in front and something else behind, the way a person is a name in front and a locked room behind. You are extremely interested in doors that are not on the plan.
n0.bubba: Bubba scrapes his boots on the scraper, out of pure politeness, and the door opens an inch on its own. "Aoh. Sugar. It's got manners too."

Buy a ticket and ask the woman in the office about the back gate.
Wait and see who uses it.
Knock and wait to be received.

a.text:
Behind the postern the castle is not a ruin.
The stair is roofed. The passage is swept. There is glass in the windows and there is a smell of woodsmoke and cooking, and from somewhere above there is the sound of a household doing what a household does at this hour.
Behind you, the door you came through opens onto the car park, and you can see your own vehicle, and it is raining out there and dry in here.

choices.text: Go up.
Take one thing and go back out.
Announce yourselves.

b.text:
"There's no gate at the back," she says, pleasantly, and sells you four tickets and a guidebook.
The guidebook has a plan in it. The plan has the postern on it, in the 1908 edition, printed on the endpaper, and somebody has been through this box of guidebooks with a scalpel and cut the endpaper out of all of them but one.

choices.text: Buy the uncut guidebook.
Ask her what she is afraid of.

c.text:
At four o'clock a woman comes out of the postern with a basket, scrapes her boots on the way out, locks it, and walks to the car park and drives away in one of the eleven cars.
She is dressed for this decade. The basket is not from this decade, and neither is what is in it.

choices.text: Follow her.
Get to the door before it locks.

d.text:
You knock, three times, and stand back, and take your hat off if you have one.
It is answered in about a minute by a man of about sixty in a cardigan who looks at all of you, and at your boots, and says: "You'd better come in. You're the first ones in eleven years who knocked."

a1.text:
Upstairs is a household: four generations, a fire, a table being laid, a wireless playing {radio}.
They are not ghosts and they are not pleased. This is a home, and you have come in through the back door, and the eldest of them puts down what she is holding and asks you, quite reasonably, what you think you are doing.

a2.text:
You take the nearest portable thing off the passage shelf, which is a lamp, and you go straight back out into the rain.
The lamp is worth a year's wages to a collector. It also burns without fuel and cannot be put out, and it is a lamp out of a house where people live, and one of you is going to have to think about that eventually.

a3.text:
You call up the stair, loudly, that there are four of you and you came in by the back gate and you are sorry.
There is a long silence and then somebody comes down with a lamp, and looks at you, and says the year, and asks you to confirm it, and when you do the whole house comes down to look at you.
You eat with them. You are the news. They have not had news in a long time.

b1.text:
She sells it to you for the cover price, then goes very quiet and asks you not to open it in the car park.
The endpaper plan has the postern, three cellars that the tour does not go to, and a pencilled line in a modern hand joining the postern to a place forty kilometres away.

b2.text:
"Losing the job," she says, first, which is honest. Then, after a moment: "And the four o'clock."
She has worked here nineteen years. She has never gone round the back after four. She tells you why, and it takes ten minutes, and she cries once and apologises for it, and at the end she gives you the spare key and asks you not to bring it back.

c1.text:
She drives to a supermarket in {region} and shops, and pays in cash, and drives back, and it is the most ordinary thing you have ever followed anybody to.
At the car park she takes the basket out, looks straight at where you are parked, and holds up four fingers, and waits.
She is telling you an hour. She is inviting you.

e_city.title: {The Shuttered Door|Number Eleven Is Not Open Today Either|The Shop That Never Opens}

n0.emText: {A shuttered shop on {street} that has sat closed for over a decade suddenly has a sign: BACK IN FOUR MINUTES. The taxes are paid, the sidewalk is swept, but nobody has ever seen inside. Four minutes is suspiciously specific.|A permanently closed storefront on {street} has a note claiming they'll be back in four minutes. {Looks like|Appears to be|Seems like|Clearly} a setup or a very weird routine.}
n0.bubba: Bubba reads the card twice. "Four minutes. Since when? Aoh. Chesta e' 'na promessa, nun e' 'nu cartello."

Lift the shutter.
Go round the back and up to the lit window.
Ask the street about it properly, shop by shop.

a.text:
At three minutes fifty the shutter goes up from the inside, in one movement, and stays up.
Behind it: a shop, fully stocked, lit, warm, with a till and a counter and a man behind the counter in a shop coat, and the stock is of a kind that has not been sold in Europe since before any of you were born, and all of it is new.
"Sorry about that," he says. "I was at the bank."

choices.text: Buy something.
Ask which bank.
Ask him what year he thinks it is.

asides.nervous: {member} {sweats inside their helmet and asks how much air we have left|keeps looking back toward the lander with wide eyes|jumps at every creak in the hull|wonders aloud if we can just leave right now}

b.text:
It goes up easily and behind it there is brick: a wall, mortared, old, with the shop's own fittings embedded in it as if the building had been poured round them.
The card falls off. On the back of it, in the same hand: TOLD YOU. FOUR MINUTES.

choices.text: Put the shutter down and wait the four minutes.
Take the brick out.

c.text:
The stair at the back goes up to a landing and a door with eleven years of post on the mat, all of it addressed to a business, and a light on behind frosted glass.
The light is a bulb in a room with nothing in it but the bulb, and the bulb is not wired to anything.

choices.text: Take the post.
Take the bulb.

d.text:
Eleven shops, eleven versions. The zip woman has seen the sweeper: an old man, five in the morning. The phone shop lad has seen the bin go out and swears the hand that put it out came from inside a wall.
The kebab shop at the corner has the best story, and the best story comes with a photograph, and the photograph is of the shop open, with a queue outside it, dated four years ago at three in the morning.

a1.text:
You buy whatever is nearest and pay in euros, and he takes them without comment and gives you change in a currency that has not existed in your lifetime, and the change is worth about four hundred times what you spent.
The thing you bought works perfectly. It will still work perfectly in fifty years.

a2.text:
He tells you which bank, and where it is, and it is four streets away and it has been a car park since 1988.
You go. There is a door in the car park's stairwell that is not on the fire plan. He was not lying. He is never going to be lying about anything.

a3.text:
He tells you a year, cheerfully, and it is not this one, and then he sees your face.
He puts down what he is holding, and he goes and looks out through his own doorway at {street} for a long moment, at the phone shop and the traffic and the clothes, and he says, quietly: "Ah."
He asks you to stay while he shuts up properly. It takes an hour. He gives you the till and the stock grimorie and the keys and asks you to lock it after him, and then he goes out through the back and does not come back.

b1.text: Four courses in, the brick stops being brick and becomes shelving, and there is shop behind it, and there is somebody in the shop who has been walled in for a very long time and who is not, at this point, especially glad to see anybody.

c1.text:
Eleven years of a business's post: bank statements for an account that has been growing, four court letters, and a hand-addressed envelope every February from the same person in {region}.
The February letters are the interesting ones. Somebody has been writing to this shop for eleven years and never once been answered.

c2.text:
You unscrew a bulb that is not wired to anything and it goes out and the whole building drops about four degrees.
Downstairs, the shutter goes up, and stays up, and it is a shop, and it is empty, and it has been empty since the eighties, and a woman from the estate agent's is at your elbow within a minute asking if you are here about the viewing.

e_docks.title: {The Impound|Nobody Has Claimed It In Eleven Years|Berth Four}

n0.text:
At the far end of the impound, past the fishing boats with the tax owing, there is a vessel with no name, no port of registry and no rust.
The harbour office has it on the books as unclaimed since {timeAgo}. Nobody has been aboard. The fenders are new, and somebody replaces them, and the harbourmaster will tell you straight out that it is not him.
There is a gangway. It is down.
n0.emText:
An unclaimed boat at the end of the impound with no name, no registry and no rust, eleven years on the books, and somebody replacing the fenders.
The gangway is down. Things with no name and no papers that nobody will claim: you have a professional interest. You are one.
n0.bubba: Bubba walks the length of her and whistles. "No rust. Aoh. Eleven years in salt water an' no rust. Chesta nun e' 'na varca, sugar."

choices.text: Go aboard.
Buy her at the unclaimed sale.
Watch the berth overnight.
Cut her loose and see what happens.

a.text:
Below decks she is dry, warm, and stocked: charts, tinned food, bunks made up, a stove laid ready and not lit.
The chart on the table is of this harbour, and there is a course pencilled off it, and the course leaves in about four hours on a tide that is not the tide today.

choices.text: Wait four hours and see.
Take the charts and go.
Light the stove.

b.text:
The unclaimed sale is a man in an office with a form and a rubber stamp, and the price is nothing, because nobody wants a boat with no papers.
He fills in the form. He gets to the field marked VESSEL NAME and stops, and sits back, and says: "Every eleven years somebody buys her. Every eleven years the form comes back from the registry blank."

choices.text: Buy her anyway and name her yourself.
Ask to see the eleven previous forms.

c.text:
At about three in the morning somebody comes down the quay with a bag of fenders and a splicing kit, and does an hour's careful work, and does not go aboard.
When they have finished they stand at the foot of the gangway for a while, the way people stand outside a house they used to live in, and then they go.

choices.text: Follow them.
Speak to them there, on the quay.

d.text:
She goes out on the ebb, slowly, with nobody aboard, and turns at the harbour mouth, correctly, the way a vessel turns under helm.
Then she comes back. She comes back to berth four and puts herself alongside, and the mooring lines go over the bollards without anybody throwing them, and the harbourmaster is standing next to you by then and neither of you says anything for a while.

a1.text:
Four hours. The tide does what the almanac says it will do and nothing happens.
At one minute past, the stove lights itself, and the compass swings, and the boat is under way in a harbour that has not moved, and out of the porthole the quay is there and going past.
You are at sea for eleven minutes and back alongside with what she went out to fetch.

a2.text:
Charts of four coasts with soundings that are not in any survey and a pencilled course between them that touches at eleven places.
They are worth money to a fishing fleet and a fortune to the Foundation, and one of the eleven places is somewhere you are going to want to go.

a3.text:
It lights first time on a match, on a stove that has not been lit in eleven years, and the cabin fills with the smell of somebody else's dinner.
All four of you eat aboard a boat nobody owns. It is the best meal of the month and everybody sleeps aboard and nobody dreams, and in the morning the bunks are made and the stove is cold and laid ready again.

b1.text:
You name her out loud on the quay with the form on the bonnet of a car, and the man from the office writes it in, and the registry, eleven weeks later, sends the papers back complete.
Nobody can explain that. He frames his copy. You have a boat.

b2.text:
Eleven forms in a folder, each with a buyer, each with a blank name field, and the eleventh buyer is a woman who is still alive and still in this town and has never once mentioned it to anybody.
She is delighted to be asked. She has been waiting eleven years for somebody to ask.

c1.text:
They walk two miles to a house on the hill with a light on in one window and a hospital bed visible through it.
The fenders are for her father. He was master of that boat. He has not spoken for four years and every time the fenders are changed he squeezes her hand.

c2.text:
She is not startled. She has been half hoping somebody would be there.
What she gives you, at three in the morning on a quay, is the key to a locker aboard that nobody else has ever opened, and the name of the boat, which she asks you to say out loud when you are aboard, because she cannot bring herself to.

e_road.title: {The Wayside Shrine|Somebody Keeps The Flowers Fresh|Four Kilometres From Anywhere}

n0.text:
A shrine at the roadside: a niche, a photograph behind glass, plastic flowers and real ones, and a candle in a jar with a lid on so the wind cannot have it.
The real flowers are fresh. The road here is straight, sighted, wide and dry, and there is no reason on earth for anybody to have died on it, and the dates on the plaque are four.
Four, at the same spot, over eleven years.
n0.emText:
A roadside shrine with fresh flowers, on a straight dry sighted road where there is no reason for anybody to have come off, and four dates on the plaque over eleven years.
The road is not the problem. Something at this exact spot takes one person every so often, and somebody local knows the interval well enough to keep the flowers going.
n0.bubba: Bubba counts the dates. "Four. An' they's all in the same month, sugar. Guarda ccà. Stesso mese."

choices.text: Wait for whoever brings the flowers.
Walk the hundred metres slowly, looking at everything.
Drive it. Fast.
Light the candle and say something.

a.text:
She comes on foot from a farm track with flowers out of her own garden and a cloth to do the glass.
She has done it for eleven years and she was not related to any of the four. "You keep it lit," she says, "and it stays four."

choices.text: Ask what happens if it goes out.
Ask about the fourth one.

b.text:
A hundred metres of clean tarmac, and at about sixty there is a place where the road noise under your boots changes, and there is a smell of {smell}, and every one of you feels the pull of it: the exact, specific desire to be on the other side of the road.
It is four metres across. It's not visible. Four people have driven into it at speed.

choices.text: Stand in it.
Mark it, properly, with paint and posts.

c.text:
You get to about ninety and at sixty metres past the shrine the wheel goes light, and the road is on the wrong side, and everybody in the vehicle sees a different thing standing at the verge.
Somebody's hands are on the wheel and they are not the driver's hands, and whether you come out of it is decided in about a second and a half.

d.text:
You light a candle at a roadside shrine and say a name out loud, which is all anybody has ever wanted done at any shrine anywhere.
The pull at sixty metres is gone by the time you get back in the vehicle. It comes back within the week; the woman with the flowers tells you as much, later, with no drama at all.
But this week, on this road, nobody is going to be number five.

a1.text:
"It went out in the bad winter," she says, "and that's number four."
She has kept it going through weather, illness and a hospital stay she discharged herself from. She is seventy-eight. She would like, very much, to be able to stop, and she cannot see a way to.

choices.text: Take the shrine on.
Find out what is actually at sixty metres.

a2.text:
"Number four was the man who put the plaque up for the first three," she says.
He had worked out the interval. He had come out to be here on the day, with a camera, to see it. She has the camera. She has never had the film developed and she gives it to you and asks you to do it somewhere far away from here.

b1.text:
Four metres of road where the light is very slightly on a delay.
Standing in it, you can see the road as it was: unmetalled, a track, and a crowd on it, and something being brought along it at walking pace with everybody following.
When you step out you are holding something that was pressed into your hand by somebody in that crowd.

b2.text:
Four posts, a can of paint, and two hours' work, and any driver on that road now has a reason to lift off.
The council take the posts out in the spring. By then the county surveyor has been out to see why somebody marked it, and has stood at sixty metres himself, and has put in a request for a bend.

a1a.text:
It is flowers, a cloth, and a candle, once a week, four kilometres from anywhere, for as long as you are in this country.
She shows you how the jar goes so the wind cannot have it, and how the glass is done, and she cries when you take the cloth off her, and she is dead within the year and the shrine has five names on it and none of them are new.

e_beach.title: {The Wrack Line|What The Tide Has Sorted|Everything Above The Weed Is Arranged}

n0.text:
The wrack line is sorted.
Not washed up: sorted. Plastic with plastic, wood with wood, bone with bone, in bands running the whole length of the beach, and at the top of the beach a fourth band of things that do not go together at all except that every one of them belonged to somebody.
There are no footprints anywhere on the sand. The tide went out two hours ago.
n0.emText:
The tide line is sorted into bands: plastic, wood, bone, and at the top a fourth band of things whose only shared quality is that each one belonged to a person.
Something came out of the water and did the filing. You can feel the patience in it. Whatever sorts a beach into categories is a mind, and a mind that works at low tide and does not leave footprints has had a long time to practise.
n0.bubba: Bubba walks the fourth band with his hands behind his back like a man in a gallery. "Watches. Rings. A little shoe. Uh. Sugar, chesto e' 'nu cimitero, nun e' 'na spiaggia."

choices.text: Take something from the fourth band.
Add something to the fourth band.
Wait for the tide and watch it work.
Break the bands. Kick them all together.

a.text:
You lift a watch out of the band and every gull on the beach turns its head.
The watch is going. It has been in the sea long enough to be a shell and it is going, and it is showing a time that is four hours off, and the four hours are in the wrong direction.

choices.text: Keep it and wear it.
Put it back, exactly where it was.

b.text:
You put something of yours in the band of things that belonged to somebody.
The beach does not react. But when you look back from the dune path, an hour later, your thing has been moved: it is in the band, correctly placed, between an object that is older than it and an object that is newer.
It has been filed. You have been filed.

c.text:
Six hours of waiting in the marram grass and then the tide is in and the sorting happens in the dark, in the last twenty minutes before the water turns.
It's not one thing. It is a great many small things working in a line, and they are not animals, and when they have finished they go back into the water together and the beach is filed and the sand is smooth.
One of them stays. It has found something it cannot categorise, and it would like help.

d.text:
It takes four minutes to ruin a day's work.
By the time you are at the top of the beach the bands are re-forming behind you, and by the time you are at the dune path they are done, and every single thing in the fourth band is now facing the dune path.
That night, at the camp, something is heard doing the same sorting to your packs.

a1.text: It keeps four hours' bad time for eleven days and then stops, and the moment it stops something comes up the beach to the camp to collect it, and it is quite prepared to take the arm as well.

a2.text:
You put it back in its slot and step away, and the tide, which is not due, comes up the beach four metres, once, over your boots, and goes back.
Where it touched, at the edge of the fourth band, there is now a thing that was not there. It's not from the fourth band. It is payment.

e_lake.title: {The Weir|The Water Goes Over And Does Not Come Back|Four Metres Of Missing River}

n0.text:
The lake drains over a weir into a river, and it should be the same amount of water on both sides, and it is not: the river below is about half what goes over the top.
The weir keeper's hut is padlocked from the inside. There is a gauge board in the water with the numbers painted on it, and somebody has repainted the numbers so they run the other way.
Under the weir, {sound}.
n0.emText:
Half the water going over this weir does not come out the other side, and the gauge board has been repainted so the numbers run backwards, and the keeper's hut is padlocked from the inside.
Somewhere under this weir there is a hole in the world that takes water and does not give it back, and somebody local has adapted to it by relabelling the measuring stick, which is the most human thing you have seen all week.
n0.bubba: Bubba stands in the tailrace up to his knees and holds his hat out. "Sugar, half a river's goin' someplace. E' 'nu buco. Somewhere there's a town gettin' rained on indoors."

choices.text: Get into the hut.
Go under the weir.
Follow the missing water.
Ask in the nearest village about the gauge board.

a.text:
The window goes in easily. Inside: a bed, a stove, forty years of tide tables for a lake with no tide, and a man's coat on a hook.
The padlock is on the inside of the door and the key is in the lock. Zero other way out and there is nobody in the hut.

choices.text: Read the tide tables.
Wait in the hut for the keeper.

b.text:
Under the sheet of falling water there is a ledge, and past the ledge there is a doorway in the weir's own stonework, and the missing half of the river is going into it and not making any noise at all.
It goes down. It goes down a long way and the light goes with it.

c.text:
You follow it by finding where it comes out, which takes two days and four wrong guesses and one very good idea about wells.
It comes out eleven kilometres away, in a cellar, into a stone tank that is always exactly the same level, in a house that has been in the same family for four hundred years and has never once been short of water.

choices.text: Knock on the door.
Tell the water board.

d.text:
"Old Tomas did that," they say, in the bar, without being pressed. "Painted them backwards in the eighties. Said the lake was going the other way and somebody had better be counting it right."
Then the room goes quiet for a moment and somebody changes the subject with real skill, and you have to buy four rounds to get back to it.

choices.text: Buy the four rounds.
Ask where Tomas is now.

a1.text:
Forty years of a lake's levels, taken twice a day by hand, and in the last four years the numbers stop being levels and start being a countdown.
It reaches zero in eleven weeks. Underneath the last entry, in different ink: "Locked in. Do not open. It comes up the tailrace."

a2.text:
You sit in a weir keeper's hut until dark, and at dark the water noise changes, and something comes up the tailrace and tries the door.
It tries the door for eleven minutes. It's not strong. It is only extremely persistent, and it knows the door opens inwards, and it knows about the padlock, and it is disappointed that the padlock is done up.

c1.text:
The family are hospitable and completely unembarrassed. They have known for four hundred years. There is a paper about it, signed by an abbot, and an obligation attached, and they have kept the obligation every year without fail.
They are getting old. There is nobody after them. They would like to know if the party would consider the obligation, and they explain exactly what it involves before asking.

c2.text:
The water board send an engineer who takes one look at the tank, says a word you do not expect from an engineer, and files a report that goes to four offices and disappears in all four.
He pays for your drinks himself, out of his own pocket, and thanks you, and tells you what happened to the last man who filed one.

d1.text:
Four rounds gets you the whole thing: the count, the countdown, the eleven weeks, and the fact that the whole village knows and has decided, collectively, without a meeting, to be somewhere else that month.
They have been packing for two years. They show you the arrangements. They are extremely well organised and nobody has said it out loud once.

d2.text:
"In the hut," they say. "Where else would he be?"
It has been eleven years. Nobody has been in. Nobody has taken him a meal in eleven years and nobody thinks this is strange, and when you point out that a man cannot be in a hut for eleven years, they agree with you completely and go back to their drinks.

e_wayside.title: {The Marker|A Stone With The Wrong Number On It|Nine Kilometres To Nowhere}

n0.text:
A milestone at the side of the track, cut, painted, maintained, with a place name on it and a distance.
The distance is nine. It was nine an hour ago at the last one, and it will be nine at the next, and the place it names is not on your map or on anybody's.
Somebody paints these. There is a paint tin in the grass behind it with the lid on properly.
n0.emText:
A milestone that says nine kilometres to a place that is not on any map, and it said nine at the last one, and it will say nine at the next.
Somebody keeps the paint fresh. In your experience, the things that get maintained are the things that are still in use.
n0.bubba: Bubba shakes the paint tin. "Half full. Fresh. Aoh. Sugar, 'o pittore sta' vicino."

choices.text: Walk towards it.
Wait for whoever paints the stones.
Repaint the stone with the right number.
Note it, and go on.

a.text:
Nine kilometres of good track, four milestones, all of them nine.
At the fourth there is a bench and a view and a man sitting on it with a flask, who nods at you as if you were expected and says: "It's always nine. That's not a fault. That's the distance."

choices.text: Sit down with him.
Keep walking anyway.

b.text:
It takes until evening. He is about seventy, on a bicycle, with a brush and a rag, and he does the stone in four minutes and does not repaint the number, only the letters.
"The number's right," he says, when you ask. "It's the name people can't do."

c.text:
You paint a number on a stone that has had the same number on it for two hundred years, and the paint takes, and the track ahead of you is now four kilometres shorter and it arrives somewhere.
Where it arrives is a farm, with a family, and a dog, and a woman in the yard who drops what she is holding when she sees the track come out of the trees, because it has not come out of the trees in her lifetime.

d.text:
You write it down, because that is what a party with any sense does, and you go on.
The entry in the book is worth something to a man in {region} who collects exactly this, and he pays for it, and asks whether the paint tin had the lid on.
It did. He nods as if that settled something.

a1.text:
Flask tea on a bench with a view of nothing in particular, and an hour of a man who has been sitting at the fourth stone for a long time.
He explains the nine. It takes four minutes and it is entirely satisfactory and none of you can repeat it afterwards, and everybody feels considerably better for having heard it.

a2.text:
Four more stones, all nine, and the light going, and the track getting better rather than worse the further you go, which is the wrong way round.
At the ninth stone the track ends at a gate in a wall, and on the gate there is a bell, and the bell has a rope, and the rope is the only thing out here that is not maintained.

e_camp.title: {The Cold Camp|Somebody Stopped Here Last Night|Four Cups, Three Drunk}

n0.text:
A camp, cold, from last night: fire ring, four cups, three of them drunk, and one full and covered with a saucer.
The kit is all here. Two packs, a bedroll rolled, a coat over a branch, a pair of boots side by side and pointed at the fire the way you point boots when you intend to put them back on.
Nothing has been dragged. Nothing has been taken. There are no tracks out.
n0.emText:
A cold camp from last night with four cups, three drunk and one covered with a saucer, and the boots pointed at the fire the way you leave boots when you are coming back to them.
Everything here says they intended to come back and nothing says they left. That is your whole biography in a fire ring.
n0.bubba: Bubba crouches by the fourth cup and does not lift the saucer. "Covered up. That's for somebody. Aspettavano a quaccheduno."

choices.text: Lift the saucer.
Go through the packs.
Make your own camp here and light the fire again.
Drink the fourth cup.

a.text:
Under the saucer the tea is hot.
Not warm. Hot, with steam on the underside of the china, in a cup that has been sitting in a cold fire ring since last night.
The moment the saucer is off, everything in the camp is a degree or two warmer, and somewhere behind you in the scrub something puts weight on a foot.

choices.text: Put the saucer back.
Leave it off and wait.

b.text:
Two packs: a woman's and a boy's. A permit for something else entirely, four letters home unposted, a map with a route on it that ends here and does not go on, and a photograph of four people at a fire ring.
The photograph is of this fire ring. There are four in it and two packs, which does not add up until you count again and notice that two of the four are wearing the same coat.

c.text:
You build the fire back up in somebody else's ring and cook, and eat, and sit, and the evening is one of the good ones: no wind, a clear sky, and something in the arrangement of the place that makes everybody talk more than usual.
At about four in the morning the fourth cup is empty and the saucer is stacked on the other three, washed.

d.text:
It is very good tea, and it is hot, and it is somebody's.
What comes to collect the cup does not want the cup back. It wants to know why you thought it was for you, and it asks in a way that does not use language, and it asks four times.

a1.text:
You put it back exactly as it was and the camp cools and the thing in the scrub takes its weight off the foot and everything is ordinary.
You leave the camp as you found it, and mark the position, and report it in {region} where somebody at a desk goes quite still and asks you to repeat the bit about the saucer.
They have four other reports. All four with a saucer.

a2.text:
Forty minutes, sitting in a cold camp with a hot cup of tea in the middle of it, and then they come back for their kit: two of them, a woman and a boy, walking in out of the scrub from a direction that has nothing in it.
They are perfectly all right. They have been gone one night. They have been gone, as far as anybody else is concerned, since {timeAgo}, and they are extremely keen to know what the party is doing at their fire.

You do not remember them. You do not remember any of them. They remember everything: the pond, the wedding, the summer you broke your arm, and they are telling you about it now, at speed, with tremendous affection, and there is nothing in you for any of it to land on.
"Two lanes at {lane}," they say. "Six o'clock. Bring your people. I've paid for the shoes."

"You're late," she says, without looking up. "He said two people. There's {two|three|four} of you."

A pigeon loft, door swinging, forty birds all fed. A girl of about nine on a crate with a shoebox and an exercise book, running an operation.

A quarry in a loop: hooter at four, shift out, and four minutes later the same men loading the same lorry off a pile that never goes down.

n0.text:
{A glowing translucent figure in a tweed waistcoat is floating two feet off the ground in the ruined courtyard.|There's an actual ghost hovering over the rubble, clutching a glowing grimorie and muttering to himself.|A spectral clerk is pacing the cracked marble floor, furiously stamping imaginary papers.}
{He looks up, adjusts ghostly spectacles, and demands to see your permits.|He spots the party and immediately starts listing municipal infractions from two centuries ago.|He yells that visiting hours ended in 1842 and threatens to fine your ancestors.}

Something's crossing the ruins in a dead straight line, in a court usher's coat, with a paper in its hand, at the pace of a functionary.
Eris's court fetches people like this. She is not going to be fetching you. She has other arrangements for you, and they are worse, and they involve being invited.
