a.text:
It walks into you and stops, exactly, at contact, and looks up for the first time.
It has a face like a passport photograph of somebody who has been dead a while. It waits. It is waiting for you to say the thing that people say to an usher, and none of you knows the thing.

choices.text: Say you are not the one it wants.
Say you will come.

asides.any: {member} {keeps an eye on the sensors and says nothing|watches the approach with a neutral squint|checks their holster with quiet efficiency|stands by the entryway, ready for trouble}

b.text:
It goes to a cellar under the third heap and stands at the top of the steps and reads out a name, once, and waits.
The name is answered. Somebody comes up out of that cellar who has been living down there, and they are shaking, and they go with it, and neither of them looks back at you.

choices.text: Go down into the cellar they came out of.
Walk with them as far as they will let you.

c.text:
It lets you. That is the thing nobody expects: it holds the paper out, patiently, like a man showing a ticket.
It is a summons out of the Court of Eris, in four languages, three of which are not used for paperwork, and the name on it has been struck out and rewritten twice. The second name is not the one it read out at the cellar.

choices.text: Add a name.
Hand it back and let it get on with its work.

d.text:
You put a court officer down in a field of rubble, which is a thing that can be done and which has consequences.
It comes apart like a coat falling off a hook. The paper does not. The paper stays in the air where its hand was, and then goes, on the same bearing, at the same pace, without it.

a1.text:
"I am not the one you want."
It looks at the paper. It looks at you. It compares, visibly, for about eight seconds, and then it steps round you, which is the first time it has deviated from the line, and goes on.
Where it stepped round you, the ground is scorched in two footprints, and there is something in the scorch.

a2.text:
You say you will come, and it takes you at your word, and the ruins fold up like a map being closed.
What you get is four minutes in a corridor outside a court that does not exist in this dimension, and a docket with your name on it that entitles you to be heard at a time of the court's choosing.
It is worth an enormous amount to certain people. It is also a debt.

b1.text:
Somebody has lived down there for a long time: a bed, a stove, four years of tins, and a wall covered in dates crossed off.
The last twenty are not crossed off. They are circled. And under the bed, in a bag packed and ready, is everything they meant to run with.

b2.text:
You walk beside a stranger to the edge of the ruins with an usher on the other side of them, and you talk to them the whole way about nothing at all, because that is what you can do.
At the boundary they thank you, and give you what is in their pocket, and go.
The usher, on the way past, looks at you for the first and only time, and does not write anything down, which one of you is quite sure is a kindness.

c1.text:
You write a name on a summons out of the Court of Eris, in pencil, because that is what is in your pocket.
It is accepted. That is the appalling part: it is accepted, and the usher turns ninety degrees onto a new bearing, and somewhere at the end of that bearing a person you have never met is going to look up.

c2.text:
You hand a dead functionary its paperwork back and it takes it and goes on.
On the fourth step it stops, comes back, and gives you something out of its coat: a token, brass, with a number on it. You have been given a place in a queue. Nobody who has ever seen one of these has been able to tell you whether that is good.

e_graveyard_father.title: {The Relic In The Crypt|Grave Robbing For Fun & Profit|The Family Vault}

n0.text:
{An overgrown cemetery on the hill, packed with leaning headstones and aggressively judgmental stone angels.|A dreary graveyard where the dead have better real estate than the living.|Weeds and ivy are choking a massive marble tomb in the center of the graveyard.}
{The iron gate to the main mausoleum is slightly ajar, with fresh footprints in the moss.|Someone clearly tried to pry the heavy brass door handles off with a crowbar.|Sensors detect high magical resonance and zero signs of respect for the deceased.}
n0.emText:
Something fell in the night, took a corner off a tomb, and killed everything within four metres of where it stopped. Beyond four metres, nothing.
You know what this is before you get close. Everybody in the world knows, because they were told on the news: the Father is in orbit and He is coming down in pieces, and the pieces do this.
You are the reason He is up there.

a.text:
It weighs nothing. It is the temperature of a hand, and it fits a hand, and holding it is like holding the moment before somebody speaks.
Whoever picks it up does not want to put it down, and everybody else can see that from their face.
a.emText:
It weighs nothing and it is the temperature of a hand and it fits your hand exactly, which is not a coincidence, because your hands are eight per cent of a woman who was made into the thing that did this.
Doesn't speak. It recognises. That is worse.
a.bubba: "Put it down, sugar. Put it down. Guardame. Look at me. Put it down."

choices.text: Keep it.
Put it down, slowly, and step back.

b.text:
The number in the parish office rings through to a Vatican field team who are four hours away and who have done this eleven times this month.
They arrive in a van with no markings, in coveralls, with a lead-lined box and a priest, and they are gentle and thorough and very tired, and they pay for information, and they ask you not to have touched it.

choices.text: Tell them the truth about whether anybody touched it.
Take their money and their questions and ask one of your own.

c.text:
You put a piece of God in a hole in a churchyard with your own hands and you say the only words anybody present can remember.
The grass comes back inside the four metres while you are still standing there. Not fast: at the speed grass grows, all of the missing weeks at once, in about a minute.
The yew does not come back. Nothing brings back a yew.

d.text:
There is a man in {region} who buys these. Everybody knows there is a man in {region} who buys these.
He pays what he says he will pay, which is life-changing, and he pays it in a car park, and he has the box open before you have counted it, and he is looking at it the way people look at things that have already decided something about them.

a1.text:
It is in the party's keeping now, and it will be for a long time.
Nothing dies around it any more. That stops the moment somebody decides to keep it, which is the single most frightening thing about the whole business: it wanted keeping, and it has been got.

a2.text:
It takes real effort and one of the others has to help.
It goes back in the crater and the crater is a crater and the yew is dead and the afternoon is an ordinary afternoon, and the party walks out of that graveyard with nothing, which is, on this particular occasion, an achievement.
The Vatican team, when they come, are told everything, and they are so grateful they cry.

b1.text:
You tell them, and they take it seriously and they take blood, and they give whoever touched it a card with a number on it and a date four months out.
The money is good. The card is better. The date is a promise that somebody will check, which in this world is close to love.

b2.text:
"How many pieces are there?"
The priest answers, because the coveralls will not. He says a number. He says it in a whisper in a churchyard four hours from anywhere, and it is not a number that any organisation on Earth can plan around, and he has been carrying it alone.

a.text:
Four courses out and the draught becomes a room: dry, floored, and lit by a window that cannot exist, because you are under eleven metres of keep.
The room is an office. There is a desk, a chair, a filing cabinet and a hat stand, and the office closed in {timeAgo} and nobody cleared it, and there is work on the desk in the middle of being done.

choices.text: Read what is on the desk.
Open the filing cabinet.
Sit at the desk and finish the work.

b.text:
The order was placed by the visitor centre's own trustees eleven years ago, on the advice of a man who is not a builder and who signed himself with a job title that is not a job.
He lives in the village. He answers the door with a drink in his hand at four in the afternoon and he says, before you have introduced yourselves: "Is it open?"

choices.text: Tell him it is not open, yet.
Ask what is in there.

c.text:
You put a hand on the brick and you talk to it, and you keep talking, and {It takes eleven minutes|Eleven minutes tick by|The playback lasts eleven minutes|Eleven minutes of audio} before anything answers.
What answers taps: four taps, evenly spaced, and then a pause, and then four more, and it is not asking to be let out. It is checking that the wall is still there.

d.text:
The Vatican take the report seriously enough to send two people in a week, which is fast, and they re-seal it properly with their own stamp, and they pay you a consultancy fee.
They also ask you never to come back to this castle, and the way they ask makes it clear that this is for your sake, and that they have been doing this a long time.

a1.text:
It is a report, half-written, on the subject of this castle, and it stops mid-sentence in {timeAgo}, and the sentence it stops in the middle of is about a door in the undercroft.
The pen is on the blotter. The ink in it is wet.

a2.text:
Four drawers, and the fourth is heavy: not files, objects, catalogued, tagged, and every tag is a place within a day's walk of here.
Whoever worked in this office spent a career taking things out of this county and putting them in a drawer, and then the office closed and the drawer stayed shut.

a3.text:
You sit down at a dead man's desk and finish his sentence in his pen, which is the most reckless polite thing anybody has ever done in this undercroft.
The window that cannot exist goes dark. The report closes itself. And in the drawer, which was locked, there is now a copy of it, bound, with your handwriting in it and a stamp from an office that closed before you were born.

b1.text:
He sits down on his own doorstep with relief and tells you the whole thing, which takes an hour and which he has not been able to tell anybody because of what he signed.
The short version: he did not brick up a room. He bricked up an appointment.

b2.text:
"An office," he says. "A working office. And a man in it who was very polite and asked me to come back on the Thursday, and I have never in my life been so frightened of a Thursday."
He gives you the original order, the invoice, and the name of the man on the desk, and the name is his own father's.

e_swamp_naguka.title: {The Bog Hermit's Deal|Swamp Gas & Stolen Goods|The Mud Trap}

n0.text:
{Deep in the swamp, an old wooden shack sits on rotting stilts, surrounded by bubbling mud and swarms of biting gnats.|A miserable shack is balanced over the swamp water, smelling of sulfur and cheap tobacco.|Out in the muck, a hermit's cabin is tied to three mangrove roots with frayed rope.}
{An old guy in rubber waders is sitting on the porch, cleaning a shotgun and eyeing your wallet.|A shifty swamp drifter is watching you through a cracked window, pretending to be deaf.|The local hermit waves you over with a rusty machete, looking for a sucker to trade with.}
n0.emText:
A ladder into the reeds, goods laid out on a plank across two oil drums, and a card in careful taught handwriting: WE TRADE. WE DO NOT COME UP FAR.
Naguka. The people who went under before there were people, and stayed, and learned our alphabet out of politeness. They will be able to smell what is missing in you. Everything that lives underground can.
n0.bubba: Bubba puts a tin of peaches on the plank straight away, no negotiation. "Manners first, sugar. Sempe. Then we talk."

a.text:
You lay out salt, batteries, wire, a knife, a tin of peaches.
A hand comes up the ladder: grey, long-fingered, entirely calm, and it takes the salt first and the peaches last, and it puts back four things that are worth ten times what you offered, because the Naguka have never once been able to work out what our things are worth and are terrified of cheating anybody.

b.text:
Down is a long way and then it is a room, lit blue, with a floor polished by a very long time, and eleven of them standing well back with their hands where you can see them, which somebody has taught them we like.
The eldest speaks our language like a careful student. "You came down," she says. "Nobody comes down. Are you lost, or are you rude?"
b.bubba: "Neither, signo'," says Bubba, hat off. "We're nosy. E chest'e' peggio." One of them laughs. The rest look at the one who laughed.

choices.text: Rude. Admit it.
Ask what they want from up there.

c.text:
You take the plank clean and you are four hundred metres off before anything happens.
What happens is that the ground under the reeds is not ground, and it has been listening, and eleven people who have never once cheated anybody take an extremely dim view.

d.text:
It takes an hour and a half of sitting on a plank at a hole in a swamp before anybody comes up, and when someone finally shows up, it is a nervous kid sent to see if you are the sort who waits.
You are. He goes down. Somebody else comes up: older, painted white and black across the eyes in a pattern you have seen on a harbour wall in the north.

choices.text: Ask about the paint.
Ask what they need that they cannot get down there.

b1.text:
"Rude," you say. "We are being rude. We are sorry."
The eldest considers this for a long moment and then laughs, once, a sound like a stone dropped down a well, and the eleven relax at the same instant, and you are fed.
You are down there four hours. You come up with a gift, an apology accepted, and the location of a second ladder that comes up somewhere extremely useful.

b2.text:
"Salt, iron, and news," she says. "And for somebody to tell us whether it is true that the Father is coming down in pieces, because we hear it through the ground and we do not know if the ground is lying."
You tell her the truth, which is that it is true. She sits down on the polished floor. Then she gives you what they have been keeping since long before there was an Empire to keep it from.

d1.text:
"The cold-country people paint like this," they say. "We met four of them in {timeAgo}. They were polite. We copied it. It is a good pattern. Is it rude?"
It's not rude. It is a black metal band's corpse paint on the face of somebody whose ancestors went underground before agriculture, and explaining that takes the better part of an hour and is the most fun anybody has had this week.

d2.text:
"Someone to carry a letter to the surface people who take letters," they say. "We have had it eleven years. Nobody would take it. It is about the water."
It is about the water. It is about what the Collective is putting in the water, measured over eleven years by people who drink it before we do, and it is the single most valuable document anybody has handed you all year.

p_paris_lisa.title: {The Small Painting|La Gioconda, Room Six|Thursday At The Gallery}

n0.text:
Room six, four hundred people, and the small painting behind the glass with the rope four metres out from it.
The attendant on the door has worked here nineteen years and she is not watching the crowd. She is watching the painting, and she is watching it the way you watch a dog you do not entirely trust.
On Thursdays, she tells you when you ask, they close room six for an hour at four o'clock. It's not in any schedule.
n0.emText:
Room six, four hundred people, and the attendant on the door watching the painting rather than the crowd, the way you watch a dog you do not trust.
They close the room for an hour every Thursday at four, and it is not on any schedule, and the painting is the most looked-at object on this planet, which means it has had more attention poured into it than anything else humans have ever made, and things that get that much attention wake up.
n0.bubba: Bubba, in a gallery, in his hat, at his full volume: "She's small! Aoh! Sugar, she's tiny! Nun ce credo!"

Ask the attendant what she is watching for.
Watch the crowd instead of the painting.
Get behind the glass.

a.text:
Four o'clock, room six, the doors shut and the crowd gone, and two conservators who are not conservators standing in front of the painting with a case open.
They are not cleaning it. They are reading it. There is an instrument on a stand pointed at her face and a printout coming off it and the printout is text.

choices.text: Read the printout.
Ask them, out loud, what she has been saying.

b.text:
"The eyes are supposed to follow you," she says. "That's the trick, everybody knows the trick. Mine is that on Thursdays they stop."
Nineteen years, every Thursday, at about four, the eyes stop following anybody, and for one hour the most looked-at woman on earth is looking at exactly one thing, and it is not in this room, and it is south by south-east.

c.text:
Four hundred people an hour and every single one of them does the same thing: they come in, they look, and at about the eleventh second something goes out of their face.
One in about forty does not do it. Those ones look, and frown, and look again, and go away troubled, and if you follow one out and ask, they will tell you: it moved.

d.text:
The glass is the least of it: it is the four hundred people, the attendant, the eleven cameras and a gallery with more guards than a mint.
You get about ninety seconds behind the rope before it goes wrong, and in those ninety seconds you are close enough to see that the craquelure on the varnish is not craquelure and that it is writing and that it is not in any alphabet used on this continent.

a1.text:
The printout is a transcript. It has been running since 1956 and there is a filing cabinet for it and the cabinet is full.
Most of it is nothing: weather, the room, the people. Four times a year it says something that is not about the room, and those four are on a separate sheet, and one of the four is about the thirty-first of December 2001.
a1.emText:
The printout is a transcript, running since 1956, and there is a cabinet for it, and the cabinet is full.
Four times a year she says something that is not about the room. Those are on a separate sheet. You read the sheet. She has been saying your name since 1956, at a rate of about once every three years, and the entries stop in January 2001.
a1.bubba: Bubba looks at the sheet, and at you, and puts his hand flat on the paper so you cannot read the last line. "Nah. Nun ce sta' bisogno. Not today, sugar."

a2.text:
They do not throw you out, which tells you a great deal. They ask you to shut the door.
"Since fifty-six," one of them says. "We rotate every four years so nobody does it long enough to be believed."
They let you hear one minute of it, through the headphones, and it is a woman's voice and it is perfectly calm and it is describing the room you are standing in from a position that is not in the room.

p_vatican_gauss.title: {Eight Hundred Metres Up|The Battery On The South Face|Nothing Approaches The Citadel}

n0.text:
The gauss battery on the south face tracks you for the entire approach.
It's not subtle. Four barrels, eight hundred metres up, moving as one, and every pilgrim on that road knows and nobody looks up.
At the checkpoint a Swiss Guard with a clipboard says: "It is tracking, not aiming. There is a difference and you will be told the difference if you make it necessary."
n0.emText:
Four barrels on the south face, eight hundred metres up, tracking you all the way in, while the crowd on the road pretends not to notice.
They took out the Father with a spear made out of your memories and then they built a wall and put guns on it, and the guns point outwards, at the road, at pilgrims, at you. Nobody in this Empire has yet decided whether you are a relic or a defendant.
n0.bubba: Bubba waves at the battery. Cheerfully. With his hat. "Salutamm'! They're watchin', might as well be polite."

Ask what the battery is for.
Take a job on the wall.
Get up onto the south face at night.

a.text:
Inside, it is a working city that happens to be a fortress that happens to be a church: laundry, kitchens, a printing house, four thousand people and a queue for everything.
In the third courtyard there is a chapel with a queue of nobody, and a Cardinal's clerk on the door who is looking for four people who are not from here and are not on any list.

choices.text: Take the clerk's errand.
Ask why the chapel has no queue.

b.text:
"For the sky," the Guard says, and does not elaborate, and then, because you wait: "Pieces come down. Some of them are small. Some of them are not, and we have four barrels because we have counted what is up there."
He has been on this gate eleven years and he can name the four biggest fragments in orbit by their catalogue numbers.

c.text:
The wall always wants hands: shot-loading, tracking crew, and the eleven-hour night watch that nobody local will take twice.
You do a week. On the fourth night the battery fires, once, at something at forty thousand feet, and you are on the rammer for it, and the shock through your boots is a thing you will be able to describe for the rest of your life.

d.text:
Eight hundred metres of face in the dark with four barrels above you that track anything moving, which you knew when you started.
You get to the emplacement. The crew are asleep, all four of them, and they should not be, and the reason they are asleep is sitting on the breech of the number two gun with its legs crossed, waiting for somebody to climb up.

a1.text:
The errand is to carry a sealed box from the third courtyard to a house four streets outside the wall, and to do it without the box being seen, and to come back and say that it was heavy.
It's not heavy. It's not anything: it is an empty box, and the errand is the point, and somebody four streets outside the wall now knows that the Cardinal's clerk has four people he can use.

a2.text:
"Because it is not consecrated any more," the clerk says. "And because what it is now is a room where the Empire keeps the things it has taken off people like you."
He is not threatening you. He is offering. Four minutes, one room, and whatever you can carry, in exchange for a favour later that he will not describe.

p_london_pillar.title: {The Door With No Plate|Guild Business, Not Guild Premises|Present And Past}

n0.text:
A door in a terrace with no number, no plate, no bell and a boot scraper worn hollow.
The houses either side are 42 and 44. This one is not 43. The rates are not paid on it because it is not on the roll, and the post office will not deliver to it, and everybody in this street knows to walk on the other side after dark and none of them can say why.
The letterbox is warm.
n0.emText:
A door between 42 and 44 that is not 43, not on the roll, not delivered to, with a bootscraper worn hollow by a great many boots.
Mages' Guild. Not premises: business. Thatcher's lot, before Thatcher, and after. Somewhere behind this door is the paperwork of the people who chose you, and the letterbox is warm, and this is the closest you have come and you have not moved for about a minute.
n0.bubba: Bubba puts two fingers on the letterbox and takes them off. "Warm. Ah. Sugar. E' 'a gente toia, chesta. This is them. You wanna do this today?"

Scrape your boots first, then knock.
Watch the door for a day.
Put something through the letterbox.

a.text:
It opens on a hall with a hat stand and a runner carpet and a smell of {smell}, and a woman with a pen who says: "Yes?" in the tone of somebody who has never once been surprised.
Behind her, the hall goes back a great deal further than the terrace does.

choices.text: Say what you want.
Ask what this is.

b.text:
You scrape your boots on a scraper worn hollow by two hundred years of people who knew to do it, and the door opens before you have knocked.
"Well," says the woman with the pen. "Somebody taught you something."
You are shown into a front room rather than kept in the hall, which is, you learn much later, a formal distinction.

c.text:
Eleven hours from a cafe window. Four people go in. Two of them come out. One of them comes out twice, eleven minutes apart, wearing different clothes and going in opposite directions.
The last one out at dusk is a man of about ninety who locks the door, checks it, and then walks past your window and, without stopping, drops a card on your table.

d.text:
You put a note through the letterbox and something on the other side takes it out of your fingers.
Four minutes later the door opens and there is nobody there and there is a reply on the mat, and the reply answers a question you have not asked anybody out loud since you were a child.

a1.text:
You say what you want and she writes it down without comment, and gives you a number on a slip, and says four weeks.
It takes four weeks. At four weeks exactly, wherever you are, whatever you are doing, you get an answer, and it is complete, and it is correct, and it costs you a favour that is not specified and which is called in eleven months later at the worst possible moment.

a2.text:
"Business," she says. "Not premises. There is a difference and it is the whole of the arrangement."
Then she offers you tea, which is the point at which you realise you are being assessed, and the assessment takes forty minutes and is conducted entirely as small talk.

p_reykyavik_horde.title: {Corpse Paint On The Harbour Wall|The Notice In White And Black|Landing Party}

n0.text:
Somebody has painted the harbour wall white and black in a pattern eight metres high, and it is not graffiti: it is a face, done properly, and it is a formal notice.
The Goblin Horde have landed. Four of them, in a fishing boat, and they are at the harbourmaster's office being extremely polite and asking about a band.
The harbourmaster has never been so frightened of anybody so courteous.
n0.emText:
Eight metres of corpse paint on a harbour wall, done properly, as a formal notice. Four of the Horde in a fishing boat, at the harbourmaster's office, being scrupulously polite about a band.
The Horde read a record sleeve from a cold country in 1993 and took it as scripture, and here they are, four of them, having crossed an ocean to ask about a band, and they are the only people in Europe more literal about their own mythology than you are.
n0.bubba: Bubba takes one look at the paint and one at the four of them and goes straight over with his hand out. "Guagliu'! Che bello! Which album?"

Take them to the band.
Ask about the paint.
Tell them the band is gone and send them home.

a.text:
Twenty minutes of translating between a harbourmaster who thinks he is being robbed and four Horde who think they are attending a shrine.
By the end of it everybody has understood everybody, which almost never happens, and the harbourmaster has agreed to a mooring fee that the Horde pay in gold because it is what they have.

b.text:
The band, such as it is, is two men in their thirties in a rehearsal room over a fish plant, and they have not played in four years, and one of them opens the door in a dressing gown.
What happens next is one of the great cultural encounters of the century and none of it is written down anywhere except in the Horde's own account, which is now four hundred pages long and treats the dressing gown as liturgically significant.

c.text:
"It is how one announces oneself," the tallest says, surprised to be asked. "You paint the face of the god of the place and then you wait to be received."
They did it at four in the morning off a rope. They have been waiting to be received since dawn. Nobody in this town knows the protocol and the Horde are too polite to say that they are being insulted.

d.text:
You tell four members of the Goblin Horde that the thing they crossed an ocean for is not here, which is nearly true and entirely unkind.
They take it with enormous dignity. They paint over the wall themselves, in white, in the rain, over four hours, and sail at dusk, and the town watches them go and does not know what it has just lost.

p_oslo_junehem.title: {Four Bars, Over And Over|The Rehearsal Room|Gods Of A Cold Country}

n0.text:
In a basement under a hardware shop, a band has been playing the same four bars for eleven hours.
You can hear it from the street. It's not practice: it is the same four bars, at the same tempo, and they have not stopped for food, water or the toilet, and the door at the bottom of the stairs is not locked.
The amp is going into the red and staying there and the valves should have gone hours ago.
n0.emText:
Four bars, over and over, for eleven hours, out of a basement under a hardware shop, with the amp in the red and the valves not gone.
They have found a loop and they are inside it and they think they are practising. This is a bubble made of music, held together by four people who cannot hear that they have stopped choosing to play.
n0.bubba: Bubba stands at the top of the stairs with his head on one side. "That's a good riff. That's a real good riff. Ma so' unnice ore, sugar. Nobody's that good."

Cut the power.
Play the resolving bar.
Listen to the whole eleven hours.

a.text:
Down there it is very loud and very hot and none of the four will look up.
Touching one of them does nothing. Shouting does nothing. Taking the guitar out of a man's hands leaves his hands playing it, in the air, at the same tempo, and the sound does not stop.

choices.text: Take the drummer out. He is nineteen.
Play the resolving bar.

b.text:
You pull the fuse in the shop above and the whole basement goes dark and silent, and it stays silent for about four seconds.
Then the four bars start again, in the dark, out of instruments that have no power, and the amp that is not connected to anything is still in the red.

c.text:
Somebody in this party picks up the bass that is leaning by the stairs, works out the missing bar in about forty seconds, and plays the resolution over the top of them.
The loop breaks. All four of them stop mid-note and look up and the silence is enormous, and the drummer is sick on his own kit, and the guitarist has been playing for eleven hours and his fingers are in a state that will be discussed by doctors.

d.text:
Eleven hours, sitting on the stairs, and at hour nine it stops being four bars and starts being something else: the room fills up, not with people, with attention, and by hour eleven there is very obviously a fifth musician.
At hour eleven and a half they resolve it themselves, and what walks out past you up the stairs is not one of the four and pauses to thank you for staying.

a1.text:
You carry a nineteen-year-old drummer up a flight of stairs while his hands are still playing, and they keep playing in the street, and they stop about four minutes after the cold air hits him.
He cries. He also, immediately, wants to go back down for the others, which is when you find out what kind of person he is.

p_napoli_camper.title: {The Yard On The Hill|Three Campers On Blocks|Somebody Else's Engine}

n0.text:
A yard on the hill with three campers on blocks, a dog on a chain that is too long for anybody's comfort, and a man who welds.
Two of the three are being cannibalised for the third. The third has a liminal engine in it, out of a coach, and he has fitted it himself with a manual he cannot read and a diagram he drew from memory.
"It works," he says. "It works twice out of four."
n0.emText:
Three campers on blocks in a yard on a hill, two being eaten to feed the third, and in the third a liminal engine out of a coach, fitted by a man with a manual he cannot read.
"It works twice out of four."
Bubba invented the engine. Bubba is standing next to you. Bubba is going to say something and this man is going to have the afternoon of his life or the worst four minutes of it.
n0.bubba: Bubba walks round the back of the camper, opens the hatch, looks in, and goes very still. "Aoh. Chi t'ha fatto sta cosa?" Then, to you, quietly, delighted, appalled: "Sugar. He built it out'a nothin'. It's wrong in four places an' it works."

Help him fit it properly.
Buy the camper off him.
Take it for a run, twice out of four.

a.text: It takes four hours and most of the good light.
a.emText:
It takes four hours and most of the good light, and Bubba does not once say who he is.
He rewires it, re-times it, and corrects the four wrong places, and the man watches every movement and asks the right questions and Bubba answers every one of them as though the man were the expert. At the end of it the engine catches first turn and holds, and the man puts his hands over his face.
On the way out, at the gate, Bubba turns round: "Signo'. It's called a liminal engine. Nun 'o dicere a nisciuno ca t'aggio aiutato."
a.bubba: "He's got it now," says Bubba, in the vehicle, looking out the window. "Chillo mo' 'o ssape. That's four campers a year he can do."

b.text:
Four hours, two burns, one argument about earthing, and a manual translated line by line by whoever in the party can do it.
At the end of it the engine catches on the first turn instead of the third, and he sits down on an oil drum and does not say anything for a while, and then feeds all of you until you cannot move.

c.text:
He does not want to sell it. He wants somebody to want to buy it, which is a different thing, and once you have wanted to buy it he will not take your money.
What he takes instead is a promise to come back through in the spring, and what you drive away in is a camper that works twice out of four and is the best-loved vehicle in {country}.

d.text:
It works. Then it does not.
The road ahead compresses, correctly and beautifully, for about eleven kilometres, and then it decompresses all at once with the camper in the middle of it, and what that does to the inside of a vehicle is not something anybody in this party wants to describe twice.

p_taranto_launch.title: {Volunteers Free Of Charge|The Armoured Rocket|Nine Out Of Ten}

n0.text:
The spaceport takes volunteers free of charge, which is advertised on the radio, and the radio does not mention the rest of it.
The rocket on pad four is armoured. Nobody armours a rocket against anything that is in the sky over Taranto.
The recruiting office is a portakabin with a queue outside it, and the queue is mostly young, and the form is one page and does not ask for next of kin, which is the single most alarming fact about the entire operation.
n0.emText:
A spaceport that takes volunteers free of charge, an armoured rocket on pad four, and a one-page form that does not ask for next of kin.
The queue is mostly nineteen. They armour it because of what is in orbit, and what is in orbit is a body, and the body is that of a god who was killed with a spear made out of your life.
n0.bubba: Bubba reads the form top to bottom. "No next of kin. Aoh. Sugar. Chest'e' 'na lista, nun e' 'nu modulo."

a.text:
The medical is four minutes. The training is a day and a half. The suit fits somebody else.
You go up on pad four in an armoured rocket with eight strangers, and what happens at four hundred kilometres is that everybody on board sees the same thing out of the same window at the same time and nobody afterwards describes it the same way.
Nine went up. Nine come down, which is not the usual figure, and the operation notes that in a file.

b.text:
Nine went up in the spring. Nine came down.
That is the official record and it is accurate and it is also the reason the recruiting officer drinks: nine came down, and only four of them were the ones who went up, and the other five have been given papers and jobs and flats and are living perfectly ordinary lives in this town under names that were assigned to them.

c.text:
"Debris," says the engineer, and then looks at you properly and decides you can take it. "Not micrometeorites. Debris. It is in a decaying orbit and it is four hundred kilometres of it and some of it is still warm."
They have plates and photographs and a chart of the orbit, and the chart is the most valuable piece of paper in this province.

d.text:
You stand outside a portakabin and tell forty young people the truth about the form and the next of kin and the nine.
Eleven of them leave. The rest stay, because they have nothing else, and one of them tells you so, at length, and she is right and you have no answer for her.
The eleven who left buy you a drink each, over four years, whenever they see you.

p_omega_lift.title: {The Goods Lift|Floor Nine Hundred And Something|Neutral Ground}

n0.text:
The goods lift on the north side of the Omega Tower is unmanned, unlocked and enormous, and the panel has no numbers on it: it has a slot for a card and a hand-written list taped beside it of what is on which floor, in four languages, none of them official.
Somebody has left a card in the slot.
The list stops at floor 411. The tower has considerably more floors than that.
n0.emText:
An unmanned goods lift on the north side of the Omega Tower, a card left in the slot, and a hand-written list of floors taped up beside it that stops at 411 in a building with far more than 411 floors.
They scrape the outside of this tower for fantablack. It is the only object on Earth that the loop bubbles will not touch. And somebody has left a card in the slot, which means somebody wants somebody to go up.
n0.bubba: Bubba gets in and holds the door. "Well, somebody left it. Sarrà 'nu invito. Or a trap. Same thing in a lift."

a.text:
Floor 411 is a market, and it is neutral ground: Empire, Collective, Guild, Horde and four things nobody has a name for, all trading, all armed, all extremely polite.
The rule of the floor is written on the wall in four languages: NOTHING STARTS HERE.

choices.text: Trade.
Ask about the floors above 411.

b.text:
Above 411 the lift stops announcing floors, and the light through the shaft grilles goes from daylight to something else, and the ride takes eleven minutes longer than the shaft is tall.
When the doors open it is on a corridor with a carpet and a smell of {smell} and a very long way of doors, and the doors have names on them rather than numbers.

c.text:
She comes back for it at four: a scraper, in a harness, with a tin of fantablack on her belt worth more than the block she grew up in.
"You didn't take it," she says, and that is the entire test, and you have passed it, and she takes you up on the outside of the tower rather than the inside.

d.text:
A tower card is worth about four months' wages to the right person and you have one in your pocket by teatime.
What you also have is a scraper stuck on the north face at four o'clock with no way down, and it takes her eleven hours to get in, and she does, and she remembers.

a1.text:
Everything is for sale on 411 and most of it is for sale legally, which is the strange part.
What you come away with is not the best thing you saw. It is the thing the seller would not explain, sold cheap, by somebody who wanted it out of their stall before the Empire's man came round again.

a2.text:
Four people refuse to answer. The fifth is a Collective buyer four drinks in who says: "Zero 412. There is 411 and then there is where the tower is actually from."
He will draw you the diagram for money. It is the sort of diagram that gets people publication orders.

p_milano_note.title: {The Strip In The Note|Counting Without Looking|The Man Who Is Not A Man Any More}

n0.text:
A man on a folding stool outside the exchange is counting banknotes without looking at them, which is a bank teller's trick, except that he is not counting: he is listening.
He holds each note by the corner, near his ear, and about one in forty he puts in a separate tin.
"The strip sings," he says. "You'd hear it too if you'd handled as many as me. They pay me by the hour to find the ones that sing."
n0.emText:
A man outside the exchange holding banknotes to his ear, one at a time, putting about one in forty in a separate tin.
"The strip sings."
The security strip in a euro note is the arcane part; the name on it is what deified Mario Draghi. He is not mad. He has been given a job by somebody who knows exactly what one note in forty is, and he does it on a folding stool in the street for an hourly rate.
n0.bubba: Bubba holds a note to his own ear for a while and shrugs. "Nun sento niente. But then I'm rich, sugar, so maybe they don't sing to me no more."

a.text:
You hold a banknote to your ear on a street in Milano and it is singing: four notes, a rest, four notes, in a woman's voice, from inside the strip.
It's not a recording. It responds when you move it. And when you say something to it, out loud, in the street, feeling like an idiot, it stops singing and waits.

choices.text: Say something to it.
Give it back.

b.text:
"The bank," he says. "Not that bank. The other one. They come Fridays."
On Friday a car comes and a woman takes the tin and leaves an envelope and does not count anything, and she has been doing this every Friday for eleven years, and she is the only person in the country who knows how many singing notes there are.

c.text:
He names a price and it is four times face value and he apologises for it, and it is the bargain of the decade.
What is in the tin is eleven notes, all of them singing, all of them different, and one of them is not singing in a woman's voice.

d.text:
It is a tin on a folding stool held by a man of about seventy.
You have it and you are round the corner in eleven seconds. Every note in it goes quiet the moment it leaves his hands and none of them ever sings again, for anybody, and on Friday a woman gets out of a car and finds an old man on a stool with nothing to give her.

a1.text:
You say your name to a banknote. The banknote says it back, in the same voice, and then says four more words which are not in any of the languages printed on it.
The man on the stool writes the four words down. He has forty pages of them. He has never once been able to find anybody who could get a note to answer.

a2.text:
You give it back and he puts it in the tin and thanks you for handling it properly, and then gives you one of the ordinary ones off the top of the stack, which he says is the only payment he is allowed to make.
It is an ordinary note. It stays ordinary for four days.

p_kola_shaft.title: {Twelve Kilometres Down|The Cap Is Welded|What Came Up In 1970}

n0.text:
The borehole is capped with a steel plate and the plate is welded, not bolted, and the welds have been redone at least four times by different hands over thirty years.
The site around it is derelict: cranes, a canteen with the tables still out, and a hut with a light on in it.
In the hut there is a man in his sixties on a folding chair with a thermos and a shotgun across his knees, and he is not guarding the site. He is facing the cap.
n0.emText:
A welded cap over the deepest hole anybody has drilled, redone four times in thirty years by different hands, and a man in a hut with a thermos and a shotgun who is facing the cap rather than the road.
Twelve kilometres down. They stopped because of the temperature, which is the official reason, and because of what the microphones picked up, which is not.
n0.bubba: Bubba looks at the welds and then at the man in the hut. "Four times. Somebody keeps comin' back to weld it again. Chi 'o ssape pecche'."

Put your ear to the cap.

a.text:
"My father did the second weld," he says. "I did the fourth. There will be a fifth and it will not be me."
He has sat here on and off for eleven years. He does not believe in anything. He is very clear about that, four separate times, and then he tells you what he hears through the plate when the site is quiet, and it is not a sound, it is a schedule.

choices.text: Sit the night with him.
Ask what the schedule is.

b.text:
The steel is warm and it carries sound the way a rail carries sound.
What is coming up twelve kilometres of borehole is regular, and it is not machinery, and about every eleven seconds it stops, and in the stop there is something that a human ear insists on hearing as a question.

c.text:
It takes two hours with everything the party has and the man in the hut does not stop you, which is the most frightening thing about the whole afternoon: he watches, and he drinks his tea, and when the plate comes free he stands up and puts his coat on.
What comes out of twelve kilometres of hole is not a thing. It is a pressure, and then a smell, and then a sound like a room the size of a country.

d.text:
The offices have thirty years of logs in Russian in filing cabinets nobody has opened since the Union came apart, and the canteen has the tables laid.
In the drilling log for 1970 there are four pages torn out and one page put back in a different hand, and it is the interesting page, and it is a transcript of the downhole microphone.

a1.text:
Eleven hours in a hut with a man, a thermos and a shotgun, and at about four in the morning the plate makes a sound and he stands up and points the gun at it and neither of you says anything for eleven minutes.
Doesn't happen. It has not happened for thirty years. He apologises for wasting your night, and gives you the fourth weld's rods, and asks whether one of you would be willing to be the fifth.

a2.text:
"Eleven seconds," he says. "Then a pause. Then eleven again. And every ninth pause is longer, and on the longer one, if you are touching the plate, you will feel it want something."
He has timed it for eleven years and written it all down in a school exercise book, and he gives you the book, because he is sixty-eight and he is tired and somebody else should have it now.

n0.text:
Four men in good coats have a woman in the back of a car outside a village hall, and there is a form on the bonnet, and they are filling it in properly.
That is the thing about the Umbra Excidii: they are not a mob. There is a form, there is a warrant, there is a number, and there will be a receipt.
The village is watching from behind curtains. Nobody in that village has come out.
n0.emText:
Four good coats, a woman in the back of a car, and a form being filled in on the bonnet, correctly, with a warrant number.
The Empire's witch-finders do not burn anybody in a temper. There is paperwork. There is a receipt. You are a witch with the largest unexplained magical capacity in Europe and you are standing eleven metres away watching them do this to somebody who probably sells poultices.
n0.bubba: Bubba steps in front of you without appearing to move. "Sugar. Aggia' penza' io. You stay behind me an' you say nothin'."

They show it to you, because that is the procedure, and it is in order, and the offence is named in Latin and the Latin means "arcane practice, unlicensed".
Unlicensed. Not forbidden. There is a licence. Nobody in this village has ever been told there is a licence, and the coats know that, and one of the four cannot look at you while you read it.

choices.text: Get her licensed on the spot.

b.text:
Four coats, one car, a village of curtains, and about eleven seconds of very fast decisions.
You get her. Getting her is not the hard part. The hard part is the next four months, and the form on the bonnet with a warrant number on it that now has your description in the margin.

c.text:
It takes a long time and four doors before anybody opens one, and then it goes quickly.
They did not report her. That is the first thing they say and they all say it. Somebody from outside reported her, and the village has a very good idea who, and by the time you have finished the fourth conversation there are eleven people in the street and the coats are visibly recalculating.

d.text:
You let it happen, which is what everybody behind the curtains is doing, and the car drives away with the form signed and a receipt left with the village clerk.
What you keep is the warrant number, which you read off the form, and which turns out, four months later, to be worth a great deal to somebody who is building a list.

a1.text:
There is a licence. It costs money, it takes four signatures, and one of the signatures can be given by any officer of the Empire present at the time of the offence.
You make them do it in the street on the bonnet of their own car. It takes forty minutes. It is entirely legal. The senior of the four signs it with a face like a man swallowing a stone, and the woman gets out of the car licensed.

a2.text:
He waits until the other three are in the car and then talks very fast.
He is four months into the job. There is a quota. There is a list and the list is filled from denunciations and the denunciations are paid for, and he has the grimorie in his coat and he wants somebody to take it off him because he is not brave enough to lose it himself.

x_vat_relic.title: {Sacred Only|The Reliquary That Stopped Working|Since The Thirty-First}

n0.text:
The reliquary in the side chapel has worked for four hundred years and stopped on the thirty-first of December 2001, and the parish has not told anybody.
The priest is saying the office in front of it every day as though nothing has happened. The candles are lit. The queue of the sick comes on Tuesdays and goes away again and nobody is being cured and nobody is complaining, and the whole thing has become a performance that four hundred people are putting on for each other.
n0.emText:
A reliquary that worked for four hundred years and stopped on the thirty-first of December 2001, and a parish keeping up the performance rather than say so.
The thirty-first of December 2001. That is the date on everything that broke. That is your date. Every dead battery in the Empire has your name on it and not one of these people knows.
n0.bubba: Bubba lights a candle anyway, because you do, and puts money in the box. "Nun e' colpa toia," he says, without being asked. "Statte zitta. It ain't."

"If I report it they take it away and close the chapel and the town loses its Tuesday," he says. "And the Tuesday is doing more than the box ever did. You have seen the queue. They talk to each other in that queue."

Four parishes in the province, four dead relics, all on the same date, and one that is not dead.
The one that is not dead is in a village nobody goes to, and it has been doing four times the work since January, and the priest there is exhausted and terrified and has started turning people away.

It is a bone, and a lead seal, and a slip of parchment, and the parchment is not a certificate: it is a receipt, with a date, and a second date after it in a different hand, and the second date is the thirty-first of December 2001.

A reading room in a building with no name on it, four desks, green lamps, and no catalogue of any kind.
You do not choose what you read. You write what you want to know on a slip, and it goes through a hatch, and something comes back, and what comes back is not necessarily about what you asked.
The man at the hatch has been there so long that the wood is worn to the shape of his forearms.

A reading room with four desks and no catalogue: you write what you want to know on a slip, it goes through a hatch, and something comes back that may not be about what you asked.
Britannia's black archive. You were born in Wimbledon in 1984 and everything that was done to you was done by this country's own people, and there is a hatch, and there are slips, and there is a pen in your hand.

He is not mad. He is a signals officer holding a line for a country that has stopped, and he has taped everything, and there are four hundred reels.

d.text:

It starts four kilometres the other way, at a house, in a yard, at a doorstep, and the ash on the doorstep is deeper than anywhere else, and the door has been open all winter.

x_var_empty.title: {The Country That Was Not There Last Year|Nothing Is Dusty|Varlenia}

n0.text:
Everything in Varlenia is clean.
Not maintained: clean, the way a shop is clean before it opens. The kerbs are unchipped. The road markings have no wear in the wheel tracks. There is a bus shelter with no chewing gum on it and a postbox with no scratches and a war memorial with names on it and no lichen.
The people are entirely ordinary and entirely certain that they have always lived here.
n0.emText:
Everything in Varlenia is clean. No wear in the wheel tracks, no lichen on the war memorial, no gum on the bus shelter, and every person here certain they have always lived here.
A country came into existence and filled itself in, and the filling-in included memories. You have the opposite condition. You could compare notes with the whole nation if any of them could hear the question.
n0.bubba: Bubba runs a thumb along a kerb and looks at it. "No dirt. Aoh, sugar. Chesta e' 'na scenografia. Somebody built a country an' forgot to age it."

choices.text: Find the oldest thing in the country.
Ask somebody about their childhood, properly.
Leave something worn behind.
Find the edge.

a.text:
It takes two days of asking and it is a chair.
It is in the back of a bar, it is worn on the arms, it has a burn in the seat, and the landlord says it came with the building. It is the only object in Varlenia with a history, and everybody in that bar treats it, without ever having discussed it, as furniture that is not to be sat in.

b.text:
He tells you about his childhood for four minutes and it is a good childhood and it is beautifully told and it has no smells in it, no weather, and no names except his own.
Halfway through he stops, and looks at his hands, and says: "I have never told anybody that before." He has told everybody that before. Everybody here tells everybody that, and it is the same childhood.

c.text:
You leave something worn: a boot with a hole, a photograph with a crease, a knife with a blade sharpened down to nothing.
Within a day there is a queue to look at it. Within four days it is behind glass in the town hall and somebody has written a card for it, and the card is the first true thing written in that country.

d.text:
The border is a customs post with a barrier and two guards and a queue of four cars, and it is entirely normal, and eleven metres past it the road has wear in the wheel tracks and the kerbs are chipped and there is gum on the bus shelter.
One of the two guards has been there since the country started. He knows. He has known the whole time and he has never said it out loud and he is extremely glad you asked.

Then she starts tearing tickets and handing them out, and she is still doing it at six.|The situation is pretty straightforward: It takes ten minutes to get the operators out of the van and about ninety seconds after that for the first four children to arrive, and by five o'clock there are two hundred people on a fair that was bought for an afternoon by one person.
She stands at the gate with the roll of tickets and watches it fill up. She does not say anything for a long time. Then she starts tearing tickets and handing them out, and she is still doing it at six.|Things are typically messy here: It takes ten minutes to get the operators out of the van and about ninety seconds after that for the first four children to arrive, and by five o'clock there are two hundred people on a fair that was bought for an afternoon by one person.
She stands at the gate with the roll of tickets and watches it fill up. She does not say anything for a long time. Then she starts tearing tickets and handing them out, and she is still doing it at six.}

d.text:
{Every stall on that fair is rigged and she rigged four more of them on top for the fun of it, and you win anyway, and what you win is a plastic thing worth about eleven cents.
She takes it, and looks at it, and puts it in her coat pocket, and does not mention it again, and it is in that pocket for years.|The situation is pretty straightforward: Every stall on that fair is rigged and she rigged four more of them on top for the fun of it, and you win anyway, and what you win is a plastic thing worth about eleven cents.
She takes it, and looks at it, and puts it in her coat pocket, and does not mention it again, and it is in that pocket for years.|Things are typically messy here: Every stall on that fair is rigged and she rigged four more of them on top for the fun of it, and you win anyway, and what you win is a plastic thing worth about eleven cents.
She takes it, and looks at it, and puts it in her coat pocket, and does not mention it again, and it is in that pocket for years.}

q_beacon.title: {The Keeper's List|What The Mast Needs|Dead Air}

n0.text:
{brokenthing} stands over {place}, dead, panels open to {ground}. {asker} is halfway up it with {instrument} and comes down without hurrying, because hurrying stopped helping {a while ago|on day two|before the party landed}.
The list of what it needs is short. It needs {qty} {material}. {sound}, and the mast does nothing about it, which is the point being made.

asides.cynical: {member} {snorts: "Great. More overpriced scrap."|rolls their eyes: "Ten credits says there's nothing useful inside."|scoffs: "If there was anything valuable here, someone would have stolen it already."|shrugs: "Let's just grab the loot before something explodes."}
asides.disciplined: {member} {follows standard breach protocol by the book|clears every corner with military precision|keeps a steady firing stance and monitors the sensors|checks the ammo count and maintains position}
asides.any: {member} {keeps an eye on the sensors and says nothing|watches the approach with a neutral squint|checks their holster with quiet efficiency|stands by the entryway, ready for trouble}

choices.text: Hand over the {material}.
Fix it out of the ship's own spares.
Ask what a working mast is worth first.

b.text:
The keeper thinks about it {for nine seconds|a while|without blinking}. Payment is named: {payment}.
The mast, it is mentioned on the way back up, was listening for what moves out here before it went dark. It has not been listening for {few} days now, and the keeper has been sleeping in shifts of one.

choices.text: That will do. Hand over the {material}.
Not at that price.

g.text:
The panels close over the new {material} and the mast comes back with a sound like a struck shelf.
The first thing it hears gets written out longhand and handed over, along with what was promised, and the keeper {stops sleeping in shifts|sleeps a whole night for once|puts the kettle on and sits down}.

f.text:
It takes {an afternoon|four hours|the rest of the light} and it is not pretty, but a governor off the ship's own stores will hold the load if nobody tells it what it used to be.
The mast comes up. The keeper pays over the odds, on the grounds that a fix that costs the fixer is a different {class of fix|kind of fix altogether|order of favour}.

x.text:
The spare that fit was not a spare. Something back at the ship will miss it at the worst possible moment, and the flywheel had one more turn in it, which {leader} finds out at close range.
The mast stays dark. The keeper says nothing, which is {worse than saying something|worse than anything they could say|the worst of the available responses}.

e.text:
The mast stays dark and the keeper goes back up it, alone, with the whistle in the rebreather keeping its own time.
{member} takes a bearing on the site {in case|for the log|without being asked}, and nobody talks for the first kilometre back.

q_stranded.title: {Two Hundred Days|The Lander At The Wrong Angle|Parts And Sky}

n0.text:
A lander sits at {place} at the wrong angle, and {asker} has been living in it {long enough to have a system|long enough to have opinions about the view|since before the last storm season}.
The ask is exact, rehearsed, word-perfect: {qty} {material}, for the {stabiliser|fuel governor|coil housing}, and then the sky again. {wrongness}.

asides.cautious: {member} {watches the perimeter with a frown: "Bad idea."|checks their weapon charge and backs up a step|keeps a finger on the safety and mutters a warning|eyes the surroundings: "This has trap written all over it."}
asides.empathetic: {member} {looks at the wreckage and shakes their head: "Tough way to go."|checks for survivor logs with a quiet sigh|hopes whoever was here got out in time|mutters a quiet condolence for the crew}
asides.any: {member} {keeps an eye on the sensors and says nothing|watches the approach with a neutral squint|checks their holster with quiet efficiency|stands by the entryway, ready for trouble}

choices.text: Hand it over and help with the fitting.
Something here is off. Look the lander over first.
Offer a lift instead of parts.

h.text:
The fitting takes an hour and the castaway's hands know the work better than the manual does.
Payment is the only coin left aboard: something learned in two hundred days of listening to {tone}, taught on the walk back to the pad, once, properly, with {the wind for a blackboard|the wind taking most of it|nothing to write on but the air}.

w.text:
The lander has never flown. The undercarriage grows straight out of {ground}, and under the hull there are {many} small heaps of the kind of kit a courier carries and a courier is never parted from.
Whatever is doing the asking has been fed by the asking for a long time.

choices.text: Back away without changing pace.
Put it down, here, where it sleeps.

t.text:
It looks like a lander right up until {the hold closes|it opens along a seam no lander has|the ramp comes down the wrong way}.
It's not {a hold|anything of the kind|a hold and never was}.

k.text: It stops pretending the moment {the first shot goes in|anybody raises anything|it is looked at properly}, and the lander shape comes off it {like weather|the way a coat comes off|in one long motion}.

l.text:
The lift is refused {fast|flatly|before it is fully offered}, with both hands, before the sentence is even finished.
Parts, it says. Parts and nothing else. Doesn't look at the party when it says it; it looks at {the pack|the straps|what is in the pack} the party is carrying.

choices.text: Hand over the {material} then.
Leave, and keep the pack on the far side of the group.

e2.text:
The lander is still in the mirrors a long way past where {the horizon|the curve of the ground|distance itself} should have taken it.
Nobody suggests going back for a second look, and nobody {has to say why|says why|asks why}.

q_cache.title: {Sealed On Purpose|The Case Under The Ice|What The Seal Is For}

n0.text:
A case of {maker}'s make sits under {remnant}, sealed, with {a dial that turns too smoothly|a latch that has been forced once already and reset|writing worn down to dents}.
{instrument} reads something inside worth the walk. {hazard}, so the walk was not free either.

asides.cautious: {member} {watches the perimeter with a frown: "Bad idea."|checks their weapon charge and backs up a step|keeps a finger on the safety and mutters a warning|eyes the surroundings: "This has trap written all over it."}
asides.impulsive: {member} has already tried the latch once, gently, as a scientific matter.
asides.any: {member} {keeps an eye on the sensors and says nothing|watches the approach with a neutral squint|checks their holster with quiet efficiency|stands by the entryway, ready for trouble}

choices.text: Work the seal properly.
Break it.
Leave it sealed.

a.text:
The seal gives the way a good seal gives: {all at once, undamaged, almost gratefully|cleanly, without argument, as if it had been waiting|in one movement, and stays whole}.
Inside, packed the way things are packed by somebody who expected to come back: everything in order, nothing spoiled, and room left at the top for {one more thing that never arrived|something that was never brought|a last item nobody carried in}.

c.text: The case opens {the hard way|badly|with a noise the whole site hears}. About half of what was shelved inside survives the opening, which everybody agrees, afterwards, is {still half|better than none|half more than nothing}.

b.text:
Whatever the seal was holding shut, it was not holding it shut against thieves.
It was holding it {IN|SHUT FROM THE INSIDE}. The case is empty now, and the air around it costs the party {something|a good deal|more than anybody says out loud} on the way back.

e.text:
Sealed by {maker}, left sealed. {member} takes a rubbing of the lid for the diary and puts {ground} back over it the way it was found.
Some walks are for knowing where a thing is, not for having it.

n0.text:
The one way through {place} is a gap wide enough for one, and something is sitting in it. Not hiding. Sitting.
It has {a bowl|a set of scales|an open crate} in front of it and patience behind it. The toll is {qty} {material}. The alternative is not discussed, because it does not need to be.

asides.aggressive: {member} measures the gap, then the thing in it, and does not share the result.
asides.calm: {member} notes that a toll implies traffic, and that traffic implies the toll gets paid.
asides.any: {member} {keeps an eye on the sensors and says nothing|watches the approach with a neutral squint|checks their holster with quiet efficiency|stands by the entryway, ready for trouble}

choices.text: Pay the toll.
Stare it down.
Go through it.

p.text:
It counts without touching, {nods once|inclines whatever that is|makes a small formal movement}, and leans back a whole hand's width, which is apparently the open position.
As the last of the party passes, it puts something of its own in the bowl and pushes it after them: change, or a tip, or a receipt. {The categories may not apply|None of those three words quite fits|Nobody decides which}.

s.text:
{It blinks first|It looks away first|Something in it gives first}.
It stands, which takes longer than it should and involves more of it than seemed to be there, and steps out of the gap, and leaves the bowl where it sits, full, as a matter the party is invited to {interpret|make of what they will|settle among themselves}.

f2.text: The stare goes wrong {somewhere in the middle|about four seconds in|at the point where it should have ended}. What is at the bottom of it looks back up the whole length of it, and the gap stops being {a toll booth|an arrangement|anything with rules in it}.

fgt.text: It stands up before the {second|third} step. There is {more of it than the gap explained|a great deal more of it than the gap suggested|more of it than there was room for}.

q_wager.title: {Stones|The Game At The Fire|Fair, Which Is Worse}

n0.text:
{asker} has a fire going at {place} and a game laid out on a flat rock: {stakegame}.
The rules take a minute to learn and a life to like. The stake is coin. The pot on the other side of the rock is {visible|real|already sitting there, which is either confidence or bait}.

asides.hedonistic: {member} is sitting down before the rules are finished.
asides.cynical: {member} {snorts: "Great. More overpriced scrap."|rolls their eyes: "Ten credits says there's nothing useful inside."|scoffs: "If there was anything valuable here, someone would have stolen it already."|shrugs: "Let's just grab the loot before something explodes."}
asides.any: {member} {keeps an eye on the sensors and says nothing|watches the approach with a neutral squint|checks their holster with quiet efficiency|stands by the entryway, ready for trouble}

choices.text: Sit down and play.
Play for information instead of coin.
Watch a few rounds from the warm side of the fire.

w2.text:
The pot crosses the rock. {asker} pays without a word and re-racks the stones for the next traveller, because there is always a next traveller.
The fire is shared for an hour on the strength of it, and the directions given at parting are, as far as anyone can later tell, {honest|entirely honest|correct in every particular}.

l2.text:
The stake is gone in {few} moves.
The game was fair. Everybody at the fire is quite sure the game was fair, which is {somehow worse|the part that stings|worse than being cheated would have been}.

i.text:
The winnings are not coin. They are {a lesson|the teaching itself|a thing that has to be shown}: the game itself, taught across the fire, once, properly, with the mistakes named as they happen.
It travels. Everything else on this rock stays where it is, but the game {travels|goes with them|packs}.

l3.text:
Somewhere in the third round it becomes clear the information has been flowing the other way.
{asker} now knows where the party landed, what the ship carries, and which of the party sleeps lightest, and paid for {none of it|not a coin of it|precisely nothing}.

v.text:
An hour goes by at the fire watching other people lose {interestingly|in ways worth studying|slowly and then all at once}.
No money changes hands in either direction, which by the local arithmetic makes the party the evening's {big winner|only winner|clear winner}.

q_specimen.title: {The One That Keeps Coming Back|A Fixed Hour|What Took Theirs}

n0.text:
{asker} wants one animal out of {ground} dead or carried off: the one that has taken {few} of theirs and will be back for more.
It comes at {a fixed hour|the same hour every day|whatever hour the wind drops}, which is the only polite thing about it. There is payment: {payment}.

asides.brave: {member} {steps up front with a weapon ready: "I'll take point."|grins and racks the slide: "Let's see what wants to die today."|is already at the hatch before anyone can argue|steps over the threshold without flinching}
asides.nurturing: {member} asks after the ones already taken, and the silence answers before anybody does.
asides.any: {member} {keeps an eye on the sensors and says nothing|watches the approach with a neutral squint|checks their holster with quiet efficiency|stands by the entryway, ready for trouble}

choices.text: Track it to where it sleeps first.
Wait for the hour and take it head on.
Not this one. Not today.

tr.text:
The trail reads like a sentence with the grammar wrong, but it reads.
It sleeps below {remnant}, downwind of its own front door, alone, which changes {the whole arithmetic of the afternoon|everything about the afternoon|the shape of the afternoon}.

amb.text: {Half an hour|An hour|Twenty minutes} into the tracking it becomes clear from the freshness of the ground that the roles have been reversed for at least {twenty minutes|half an hour|some time now}.

head.text: {It is punctual|It arrives on the hour|It comes when they said it would}. That is the last thing about the next ten minutes that goes to {anybody's plan|the plan|plan at all}.

e3.text:
{asker} nods like somebody filing an answer with all the other answers.
The fire gets built up a little higher for the coming hour, and the party is a long way off before it {burns down|goes out|is out}.

qe_pump.title: {The Pump|Dead Iron At The Worst Hour|What The Yard Needs}

n0.text:
The pump at {place} has died at the worst possible point of the week, {weather}, and {stranger} is standing over it holding {tool} in a way that says {tool} has already been tried.
What it needs is {qty} {material}. The merchant that stocks it is {distance}, and shut on account of {misfortune}, and the trough line goes dry by dark.

asides.nurturing: {member} has the side panel off before anybody has agreed to anything.
asides.cynical: {member} {snorts: "Great. More overpriced scrap."|rolls their eyes: "Ten credits says there's nothing useful inside."|scoffs: "If there was anything valuable here, someone would have stolen it already."|shrugs: "Let's just grab the loot before something explodes."}
asides.any: {member} {keeps an eye on the sensors and says nothing|watches the approach with a neutral squint|checks their holster with quiet efficiency|stands by the entryway, ready for trouble}

choices.text: Hand over the {material}.
Strip it down and machine the part from scrap.
Man the hand pump until the job is done, however long that is.

g.text:
The part goes in, the pump picks up mid-stroke like it never stopped, and the yard comes back to life around it.
Payment is {payment}, pressed on the party over two refusals, and dinner is not optional {either|and is not up for discussion|at all}.

f.text:
There is a part in the scrap pile that has never heard of the pump but can be talked into the job with a file and an hour.
It runs rough and it runs. {stranger} watches the whole operation like a sermon and pays over the asking, {on principle|out of principle|because it was done properly}.

x.text:
The flywheel had one more turn in it, which {leader} finds out with the smallest bone in one hand.
The pump stays dead. The dinner happens anyway, out of guilt, and is very good, which does not entirely settle {the grimorie|matters|it}.

m.text:
Two hours on the hand pump in shifts, {weather}, with the light going.
The trough line holds. By the end half the district has come past to watch, and the party leaves with more invitations than it can eat through in a month.

qe_debt.title: {Forty Minutes Ahead Of The Bailiff|The Boxes On The Step|Small Arithmetic}

n0.text:
{stranger} is on the step of a house at {place} with the door open behind and everything they own in {few} boxes.
The bailiff is forty minutes away by {vehicle}. The debt is real and the arithmetic is small, and the house is not small, and that is the whole story in one sentence.

asides.empathetic: {member} {looks at the wreckage and shakes their head: "Tough way to go."|checks for survivor logs with a quiet sigh|hopes whoever was here got out in time|mutters a quiet condolence for the crew}
asides.cynical: {member} {snorts: "Great. More overpriced scrap."|rolls their eyes: "Ten credits says there's nothing useful inside."|scoffs: "If there was anything valuable here, someone would have stolen it already."|shrugs: "Let's just grab the loot before something explodes."}
asides.any: {member} {keeps an eye on the sensors and says nothing|watches the approach with a neutral squint|checks their holster with quiet efficiency|stands by the entryway, ready for trouble}

choices.text: Pay it.
Read the paperwork. Paperwork always has a flaw.
Say nothing about money and carry boxes.

p2.text:
The bailiff arrives to a settled grimorie and hates it, quietly, {in a van|from the gate|with the engine running}, for some time.
Nobody inside the house says thank you more than once, because more than once would mean starting to cry, and there is {a kettle on instead|tea instead|a kettle going instead}.

t2.text:
The flaw is in the dates, where the flaws live. The debt is real; this WEEK'S seizure is not, and {leader} explains why in the doorway with the paper held at reading distance.
The bailiff, to his credit, checks, swears once with feeling, and leaves. Everyone understands this is a postponement. A postponement is {a currency|worth having|not nothing}.

t3.text:
The arithmetic holds all the way down. Whoever drew this up has been to the same school as the flaw and got there first.
The party stays for the loading anyway. There is a right way to {carry a box out of a house|empty a house|do this} and it involves not being alone {while it happens|for it|when it happens}.

c2.text:
{few} boxes, one van borrowed off a neighbour, one dog that rides in the front or nowhere.
At the end {stranger} shakes every hand twice and gives the party {payment}, and will not hear a word about it.

n0.text:
A cart is in the ford at {place} to the axle, and {animal} that pulled it in has developed strong views about pulling it out.
{stranger} is up to the knees in it, holding the bridle, the load, and their temper, in descending order of success. {weather}, which is not helping.

asides.calm: {member} rolls up both sleeves in a way that has ended arguments before.
asides.hedonistic: {member} points out, from the bank, that the water looks cold, which is confirmed from the water.
asides.any: {member} {keeps an eye on the sensors and says nothing|watches the approach with a neutral squint|checks their holster with quiet efficiency|stands by the entryway, ready for trouble}

choices.text: Get behind it and heave.
Take {animal}'s head and talk it round.
Walk on.

h2.text:
The cart comes out on the third heave with a sound like a boot leaving deep mud, scaled up.
{stranger} insists on payment with the stubbornness of somebody who has decided the story needs a proper ending: {payment}, and names to go with it, and the promise of a dry seat by the fire at the next farm along.

w3.text:
{animal} listens the way they listen: sideways, one ear, ready to disagree.
Then it leans into the collar like the whole argument never happened and walks the cart out at its own pace, and {stranger} looks at {leader} as if witchcraft has been performed, which is left uncorrected.

hx.text:
The cart comes out. One boot does not, for a while, and the water gets its full say in the matter before everything is back on dry ground.
The thanks are real and so is {the cold|the cold, for hours afterwards}.

e4.text:
The view back from the next rise: the cart still in the ford, {smaller now|further off|no smaller than it looked}, and the sound of the argument continuing without any need of the party's opinion.
Some afternoons belong to {other people|somebody else|other people entirely}.

n0.text:
Snares on posted ground at {place}: {few} of them, set {this morning|recently|badly, which is its own kind of cruelty}, and one of them holding something still alive.
The land belongs to {stranger}, by {sign} on the gate. Whoever set the wire will be back before dark.

asides.empathetic: {member} {looks at the wreckage and shakes their head: "Tough way to go."|checks for survivor logs with a quiet sigh|hopes whoever was here got out in time|mutters a quiet condolence for the crew}
asides.aggressive: {member} has picked out a waiting spot with a view of the gate and is standing in it.
asides.any: {member} {keeps an eye on the sensors and says nothing|watches the approach with a neutral squint|checks their holster with quiet efficiency|stands by the entryway, ready for trouble}

choices.text: Spring the snares and free what is in them.
Wait for the one who set them.
Take the catch and the wire both.

s2.text:
The wire comes off {few} pegs without a single one snapping back, and the live one is gone into the hedge before the coat is back on.
Good wire, this. It goes in the pack, on the reasoning that it has resigned from its {previous employment|last job|former line of work}.

sx.text:
The {last|third} snare has a temper. The wire whips, and takes its fee out of the back of a hand on its way past.
The animal gets away clean, which everybody involved, including the hand, rules {a fair trade|a fair exchange|about right}.

fight.text: Whoever comes over the stile at dusk comes armed for {wire and rabbits|rabbits|an empty field} and finds the afternoon has other plans.

theft.text:
The catch, the wire, and the pegs, all of it, gone inside {ten|fifteen} minutes.
Somewhere behind, a poacher is going to stand in an empty field working out that somebody has poached the poaching, and there is a small ugly satisfaction in that which does not entirely survive {the walk|the walk back|the first mile of it}.

qe_stall.title: {Short A Roof|Open To The Sky|The Missing Course}

n0.text:
A roof at {place} stands open to the sky with {stranger} on top of it, and the yard below says the job stopped mid-course: trestles out, ladder up, nothing moving.
The job is short {qty} {material}. The supplier is {distance}, and between here and there is {misfortune}, and the sky is not going to wait on any of it.

asides.disciplined: {member} {follows standard breach protocol by the book|clears every corner with military precision|keeps a steady firing stance and monitors the sensors|checks the ammo count and maintains position}
